name: Proton crossing a field line
statement: A proton ($q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) moves at $2.0\times10^{5}$ m/s straight across a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.50$ T, so its velocity is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$. Find the magnitude of the magnetic force on the proton, in N.
solution: For a charge moving perpendicular to the field, $F = qvB$. So $F = (1.6\times10^{-19})(2.0\times10^{5})(0.50) = 1.6e-14$ N.

name: Electron at 30 degrees
statement: An electron travels at $3.0\times10^{6}$ m/s in a uniform field of $0.20$ T, with its velocity making a $30^\circ$ angle with $\vec{B}$. Use $|q| = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C. Find the magnitude of the magnetic force, in N.
solution: Only the component of $\vec{v}$ perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ matters: $F = qvB\sin\theta$. Then $F = (1.6\times10^{-19})(3.0\times10^{6})(0.20)\sin 30^\circ = 4.8e-14$ N.

name: Straight wire in a magnet gap
statement: A straight copper wire of length $0.40$ m carries $5.0$ A through the gap of a magnet where the field is $0.30$ T and points perpendicular to the wire. Find the force on the wire, in N.
solution: For a straight wire perpendicular to a uniform field, $F = BIL$. So $F = (0.30)(5.0)(0.40) = 0.6$ N.

name: Tilted transmission line
statement: A $2.5$ m section of transmission line carries $12$ A. The Earth-scale field in the region is $0.050$ T and makes a $60^\circ$ angle with the wire. Find the magnitude of the magnetic force on this section, in N.
solution: Use $F = BIL\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ the angle between the current direction and $\vec{B}$: $F = (0.050)(12)(2.5)\sin 60^\circ = 1.299$ N.

name: Radius of a proton orbit
statement: A proton ($m = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg, $q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) enters a uniform $0.50$ T field perpendicular to the field lines at $1.0\times10^{6}$ m/s. Find the radius of its circular path, in m.
solution: The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: $qvB = mv^2/r$, so $r = mv/(qB)$. Then $r = (1.67\times10^{-27})(1.0\times10^{6})/[(1.6\times10^{-19})(0.50)] = 0.02088$ m.

name: Cyclotron period of an electron
statement: An electron ($m = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg) circulates in a uniform field of $0.010$ T. Find the period of its orbit, in s.
solution: From $r = mv/(qB)$ and $T = 2\pi r/v$, the period $T = 2\pi m/(qB)$ is independent of speed. So $T = 2\pi(9.11\times10^{-31})/[(1.6\times10^{-19})(0.010)] = 3.577e-09$ s.

name: Cyclotron frequency
statement: A cyclotron uses a $1.5$ T field to accelerate protons ($m = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg). Find the cyclotron frequency, in Hz.
solution: The cyclotron frequency is $f = qB/(2\pi m)$, independent of the proton's speed. So $f = (1.6\times10^{-19})(1.5)/[2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})] = 2.287e+07$ Hz.

name: Velocity selector setting
statement: In a velocity selector the electric field is $2.4\times10^{5}$ V/m and the magnetic field is $0.30$ T, with $\vec{E}$, $\vec{B}$, and $\vec{v}$ mutually perpendicular. Find the speed of the charges that pass through undeflected, in m/s.
solution: Undeflected means the electric and magnetic forces cancel: $qE = qvB$, so $v = E/B$ regardless of charge or mass. Then $v = 2.4\times10^{5}/0.30 = 8e+05$ m/s.

name: Two parallel bus bars
statement: Two long parallel bus bars are $5.0$ cm apart and each carries $10$ A in the same direction. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the force per unit length between them, in N/m.
solution: One wire's field at the other is $B = \mu_0 I_1/(2\pi d)$, and $F/L = I_2 B$, giving $F/L = \mu_0 I_1 I_2/(2\pi d)$. So $F/L = (2\times10^{-7})(10)(10)/0.050 = 0.0004$ N/m, attractive.

name: Magnetic moment of a coil
statement: A flat coil of $50$ turns, each enclosing $0.010$ m$^2$, carries $2.0$ A. Find the magnitude of its magnetic dipole moment, in A$\cdot$m$^2$.
solution: The dipole moment of a flat coil is $\mu = NIA$. So $\mu = (50)(2.0)(0.010) = 1$ A$\cdot$m$^2$.

name: Torque on a galvanometer coil
statement: A galvanometer coil has $100$ turns of area $0.020$ m$^2$ and carries $0.50$ A. It sits in a $0.30$ T field with the coil's plane parallel to $\vec{B}$. Find the torque on the coil, in N$\cdot$m.
solution: Torque is $\tau = \mu B\sin\theta = NIAB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the coil normal and $\vec{B}$. With the plane parallel to $\vec{B}$ the normal is perpendicular to it, so $\theta = 90^\circ$ and $\tau = (100)(0.50)(0.020)(0.30) = 0.3$ N$\cdot$m.

name: Tilted current loop
statement: A $20$-turn loop of area $0.015$ m$^2$ carries $3.0$ A in a uniform $0.40$ T field. The normal to the loop makes a $30^\circ$ angle with $\vec{B}$. Find the torque on the loop, in N$\cdot$m.
solution: With $\theta$ measured from the coil normal to $\vec{B}$, $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta = (20)(3.0)(0.015)(0.40)\sin 30^\circ = 0.18$ N$\cdot$m.

name: Mass from a spectrometer radius
statement: A singly charged ion ($q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) enters a $0.40$ T field at $1.2\times10^{5}$ m/s perpendicular to the field and follows a circle of radius $0.25$ m. Find the ion's mass, in kg.

name: Rod on rails
statement: A $50$ g copper rod rests on horizontal frictionless rails $0.30$ m apart. A vertical $0.60$ T field fills the region, and $8.0$ A flows through the rod. Find the rod's acceleration, in m/s$^2$.
solution: The rod is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, so $F = BIL = (0.60)(8.0)(0.30) = 1.44$ N. Then $a = F/m = 1.44/0.050 = 28.8$ m/s$^2$.

name: Floating a wire
statement: A horizontal wire has a mass per unit length of $0.020$ kg/m. It lies perpendicular to a horizontal $0.40$ T field. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the current needed for the magnetic force to support the wire's weight, in A.
solution: Per unit length, $BI = \lambda g$, so $I = \lambda g/B$. Then $I = (0.020)(9.8)/0.40 = 0.49$ A, directed so that $I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$ points up.

name: Pitch of a helix
statement: A proton ($m = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg) enters a uniform $0.20$ T field at $4.0\times10^{5}$ m/s, with its velocity $30^\circ$ from the field direction. It follows a helix. Find the pitch (the advance along $\vec{B}$ per turn), in m.
solution: The component along $\vec{B}$ is unaffected by the magnetic force, so the particle drifts at $v\cos 30^\circ$ while circling with period $T = 2\pi m/(qB) = 3.279e-07$ s. The pitch is $p = v\cos 30^\circ\,T = 0.1136$ m.

name: Energy from orbit radius
statement: A proton ($m = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg) circles with radius $0.10$ m in a uniform $0.50$ T field. Find its kinetic energy, in J.
solution: From $r = mv/(qB)$, $v = qBr/m = 4.79e+06$ m/s. Then $K = \tfrac12 mv^2 = 1.916e-14$ J.

name: Accelerated ion in a spectrometer
statement: A singly charged ion starts from rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of $2000$ V, then enters a $0.50$ T field perpendicular to its velocity and bends on a circle of radius $0.15$ m. Find the ion's mass, in kg.
solution: Acceleration gives $qV = \tfrac12 mv^2$, and bending gives $r = mv/(qB)$. Eliminating $v$: $m = qB^2r^2/(2V)$. So $m = (1.6\times10^{-19})(0.50)^2(0.15)^2/(2\cdot 2000) = 2.25e-25$ kg.

name: Antiparallel currents
statement: Two long parallel wires $8.0$ cm apart carry $15$ A and $25$ A in opposite directions. Find the magnitude of the force per unit length on each wire, in N/m.
solution: The magnitude is $F/L = \mu_0 I_1 I_2/(2\pi d) = (2\times10^{-7})(15)(25)/0.080 = 0.0009375$ N/m. Antiparallel currents repel.

name: Three parallel wires
statement: Three long parallel wires lie in a plane. Wire A at $x = 0$ carries $10$ A in the $+y$ direction, wire B at $x = 0.20$ m carries $10$ A in the $-y$ direction, and wire C at $x = 0.10$ m carries $5.0$ A in the $+y$ direction. Find the magnitude of the force per unit length on wire C, in N/m.
solution: Each of A and B is $0.10$ m from C, so each exerts $\mu_0 I_A I_C/(2\pi d) = 0.0001$ N/m. A (parallel to C) attracts C toward $-x$; B (antiparallel) repels C, also toward $-x$. The two add: $F/L = 0.0002$ N/m.

name: Work to rotate a dipole
statement: A current loop with magnetic moment $0.50$ A$\cdot$m$^2$ sits in a uniform $0.20$ T field, initially aligned with the field. Find the work an external agent must do to rotate it until its moment is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, in J.
solution: The dipole energy is $U = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B} = -\mu B\cos\theta$. Going from $\theta = 0$ to $90^\circ$ changes $U$ from $-\mu B$ to $0$, so $W = \mu B = (0.50)(0.20) = 0.1$ J.

name: Force on a semicircular wire
statement: A wire is bent into a semicircle of radius $0.10$ m and carries $4.0$ A. It lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform $0.25$ T field. Find the magnitude of the net magnetic force on the semicircle, in N.
solution: For a uniform field the net force depends only on the vector from one end to the other: $\vec{F} = I\vec{L}_{\text{eff}}\times\vec{B}$, with $L_{\text{eff}} = 2R = 0.20$ m. So $F = (0.25)(4.0)(0.20) = 0.2$ N.

name: Maximum cyclotron energy
statement: A cyclotron with dee radius $0.50$ m uses a $1.2$ T field on protons ($m = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg). Protons leave when their orbit radius equals the dee radius. Find their kinetic energy at extraction, in J.

name: Magnetic levitation of a wire
statement: A long horizontal wire with mass per unit length $0.010$ kg/m floats $1.0$ cm directly above a second long wire that is fixed to the bench. The two carry equal currents. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the current, in A.
solution: For the upper wire to float, the wires must repel (antiparallel currents) with $\mu_0 I^2/(2\pi d) = \lambda g$. Solving, $I = \sqrt{2\pi d\lambda g/\mu_0} = 70$ A.

name: Deflection through a field slab
statement: A proton ($m = 1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg) moving at $1.0\times10^{6}$ m/s enters a slab of uniform $0.10$ T field. The slab is $5.0$ cm thick, the field is perpendicular to the proton's velocity, and the proton enters perpendicular to the slab face. Find the angle by which its direction is deflected on exiting, in degrees.
solution: Inside the slab the path is a circular arc of radius $r = mv/(qB) = 0.1044$ m. Entering along the normal, after penetrating depth $w$ the velocity has turned by $\theta$ with $\sin\theta = w/r$. So $\theta = \arcsin(0.050/0.1044) = 28.6^\circ$.

name: Helical electron beam
statement: A $100$ eV electron ($m = 9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $1$ eV $= 1.6\times10^{-19}$ J) enters a uniform $2.0\times10^{-3}$ T field at $45^\circ$ to the field lines. Find the pitch of the resulting helix, in m.
solution: The speed is $v = \sqrt{2K/m} = 5.927e+06$ m/s and the cyclotron period is $T = 2\pi m/(qB) = 1.789e-08$ s. The pitch is $p = v\cos 45^\circ\,T = 0.07496$ m.

name: Separating neon isotopes
statement: Singly charged $^{20}$Ne and $^{22}$Ne ions (masses $20u$ and $22u$ with $u = 1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg) are accelerated from rest through $3000$ V and then bent through a half circle by a $0.30$ T field before striking a detector plate. Find the separation of the two landing spots, in m.
solution: With $qV = \tfrac12 mv^2$ and $r = mv/(qB)$, $r = \sqrt{2mV/q}/B$, giving $r_{20} = 0.11762$ m and $r_{22} = 0.12336$ m. The ions land a diameter from the entry slit, so the spots are $2(r_{22}-r_{20}) = 0.01148$ m apart.

name: Starting a rod against friction
statement: A $0.20$ kg rod lies across horizontal rails $0.40$ m apart in a vertical $0.50$ T field. The coefficient of static friction between rod and rails is $0.30$. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the minimum current that will start the rod sliding, in A.
solution: The magnetic force $BIL$ is horizontal; it must overcome $f_{\max} = \mu_s mg$. So $I = \mu_s mg/(BL) = (0.30)(0.20)(9.8)/[(0.50)(0.40)] = 2.94$ A.

name: Oscillating current loop
statement: A coil of $200$ turns, area $4.0\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$, carries $0.50$ A and hangs so it can rotate about a vertical axis in a horizontal $0.020$ T field. Its moment of inertia about that axis is $1.2\times10^{-6}$ kg$\cdot$m$^2$. Find the period of small oscillations about the aligned position, in s.
solution: The restoring torque is $\tau = -\mu B\sin\theta \approx -\mu B\theta$ for small $\theta$, which is angular simple harmonic motion with $\omega = \sqrt{\mu B/I}$. Here $\mu = NIA = 0.04$ A$\cdot$m$^2$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(\mu B)} = 0.2433$ s.

name: Cycloid in crossed fields
statement: A proton is released from rest in a region with a uniform electric field $E = 1.0\times10^{4}$ V/m and a uniform magnetic field $B = 0.20$ T perpendicular to $\vec{E}$. Find the maximum speed the proton reaches, in m/s.
solution: Work in the frame drifting at $v_d = E/B$ perpendicular to both fields; there the electric field vanishes and the proton simply circles at constant speed. Since it starts at rest in the lab, its speed in the drift frame is $v_d$, so in the lab its speed ranges from $0$ to $2v_d$. Thus $v_{\max} = 2E/B = 1e+05$ m/s.

name: Field beside a long wire
statement: A long straight wire carries $5.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the magnetic field magnitude $10$ cm from the wire, in T.
solution: Integrating Biot-Savart along an infinite straight wire gives $B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$. So $B = (2\times10^{-7})(5.0)/0.10 = 1e-05$ T.

name: Center of a single loop
statement: A circular loop of radius $5.0$ cm carries $3.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the loop, in T.
solution: Every element of the loop is a distance $R$ from the center with $d\vec{s}\perp\hat{r}$, so $B = \mu_0 I/(2R)$. Then $B = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.0)/(2\cdot 0.050) = 3.77e-05$ T.

name: Center of a multi-turn coil
statement: A flat coil of $100$ turns and radius $10$ cm carries $0.20$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at its center, in T.
solution: Each turn contributes $\mu_0 I/(2R)$, so $B = \mu_0 NI/(2R) = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(100)(0.20)/(2\cdot0.10) = 0.0001257$ T.

name: On the axis of a loop
statement: A circular loop of radius $10$ cm carries $4.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field on the axis at a point $10$ cm from the center of the loop, in T.

name: Where the field drops to a value
statement: A long straight wire carries $20$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the distance from the wire at which the field magnitude is $4.0\times10^{-5}$ T, in m.

name: Semicircular arc
statement: A wire carrying $6.0$ A is bent into a semicircle of radius $4.0$ cm; the straight leads run radially away from the center. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the semicircle, in T.
solution: Radial segments have $d\vec{s}\parallel\hat{r}$ and contribute nothing. The semicircle gives half a full loop: $B = \mu_0 I/(4R) = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(6.0)/(4\cdot0.040) = 4.712e-05$ T.

name: Quarter arc
statement: A quarter-circle arc of radius $2.0$ cm carries $8.0$ A, with straight radial leads at each end. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of curvature, in T.
solution: A fraction $\theta/2\pi$ of a loop gives $B = \mu_0 I\theta/(4\pi R)$; for a quarter circle this is $\mu_0 I/(8R) = 6.283e-05$ T.

name: Midpoint between antiparallel wires
statement: Two long parallel wires $20$ cm apart each carry $10$ A, in opposite directions. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude at the midpoint between them, in T.
solution: Each wire is $0.10$ m away and gives $\mu_0 I/(2\pi r) = 2.0\times10^{-5}$ T. For opposite currents the two fields point the same way at the midpoint, so they add: $B = 4e-05$ T.

name: Current for a target field
statement: A single circular loop of radius $2.0$ cm must produce $1.0\times10^{-3}$ T at its center. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the required current, in A.

name: Field near a welding cable
statement: A straight welding cable carries $100$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude $2.0$ cm from the cable, in T.
solution: Treating the cable as a long straight wire, $B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r) = (2\times10^{-7})(100)/0.020 = 0.001$ T.

name: Finite wire segment
statement: A straight wire segment of length $1.0$ m carries $10$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at a point $10$ cm from the wire, on the perpendicular bisector of the segment, in T.
solution: Biot-Savart for a finite segment gives $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_2-\sin\theta_1)$. On the bisector this is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{(L/2)^2+d^2}} = 1.961e-05$ T, slightly less than the infinite-wire value $2.0\times10^{-5}$ T.

name: Semi-infinite wire
statement: A long wire carrying $12$ A runs in from far away and stops at a point $P_0$ (the current is drained there by a large electrode). Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at a point $5.0$ cm from the wire's end, on the line perpendicular to the wire through $P_0$, in T.
solution: Use $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\theta_2-\sin\theta_1)$ with limits $0$ and $90^\circ$, giving exactly half the infinite-wire value: $B = \mu_0 I/(4\pi d) = 2.4e-05$ T.

name: Center of a square loop
statement: A square loop of side $20$ cm carries $5.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the square, in T.
solution: Each side is a finite segment at distance $a/2$ subtending $\pm45^\circ$, contributing $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(a/2)}(2\sin45^\circ)$. Four sides add: $B = \dfrac{2\sqrt2\,\mu_0 I}{\pi a} = 2.828e-05$ T.

name: Center of a triangular loop
statement: An equilateral triangular loop of side $15$ cm carries $6.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the triangle, in T.
solution: For a regular $N$-gon of side $s$, summing the finite-segment result over the sides gives $B = \dfrac{N\mu_0 I\sin(\pi/N)\tan(\pi/N)}{\pi s}$. With $N = 3$ this is $9\mu_0 I/(2\pi s) = 7.2e-05$ T.

name: Off-axis point near two wires
statement: Two long parallel wires are $0.50$ m apart. Wire 1 carries $6.0$ A and wire 2 carries $8.0$ A, both out of the page. Point $P$ lies $0.30$ m from wire 1 and $0.40$ m from wire 2. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude at $P$, in T.
solution: Since $0.30^2+0.40^2 = 0.50^2$, the lines from the wires to $P$ are perpendicular, so the two fields (each perpendicular to its own line) are also perpendicular. With $B_1 = 4e-06$ T and $B_2 = 4e-06$ T, $B = \sqrt{B_1^2+B_2^2} = 5.657e-06$ T.

name: Helmholtz pair
statement: A Helmholtz pair consists of two coaxial coils of radius $0.20$ m, each with $100$ turns carrying $1.5$ A in the same sense, separated by a distance equal to their radius. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the midpoint on the axis, in T.
solution: Each coil is $R/2$ from the center, so $B = 2\cdot\dfrac{\mu_0 NIR^2}{2(R^2+R^2/4)^{3/2}} = \left(\tfrac45\right)^{3/2}\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{R} = 0.0006744$ T.

name: Concentric opposing loops
statement: Two concentric coplanar circular loops of radii $5.0$ cm and $10$ cm each carry $2.0$ A, but in opposite senses. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude at the common center, in T.
solution: Each loop gives $\mu_0 I/(2R)$ at the center, and the opposite senses make the two fields antiparallel. So $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1}-\dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) = 1.257e-05$ T, directed like the smaller loop's field.

name: A 120 degree arc
statement: A wire carries $5.0$ A along two straight radial leads joined by a $120^\circ$ circular arc of radius $6.0$ cm. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of curvature, in T.
solution: The radial leads contribute nothing since $d\vec{s}\times\hat{r} = 0$ there. The arc gives $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I\theta}{4\pi R}$ with $\theta = 2\pi/3$, so $B = 1.745e-05$ T.

name: Hairpin with a semicircle
statement: A wire carries $10$ A in from infinity along the $-x$ axis, bends into a semicircle of radius $5.0$ cm centered at the origin, and then continues out to infinity along the $+x$ axis. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude at the origin, in T.
solution: The semicircle gives $\mu_0 I/(4R) = 6.283e-05$ T. Each straight piece is semi-infinite with the field point on its line extended, at perpendicular distance $R$: each gives $\mu_0 I/(4\pi R)$. All three contributions point the same way, so $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R}+\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} = 0.0001028$ T.

name: Single current sheet
statement: A very large flat sheet carries a uniform surface current density of $50$ A/m. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude just outside the sheet, in T.
solution: Building the sheet from parallel wires, the components along the current cancel and the rest add to a uniform field $B = \mu_0 K/2$ on each side, reversing direction across the sheet. So $B = 3.142e-05$ T.

name: Two opposing sheets
statement: Two large parallel sheets each carry a uniform surface current of $200$ A/m, in opposite directions. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude in the region between them, in T.
solution: Each sheet alone gives $\mu_0 K/2$. Between the sheets the two contributions point the same way and add to $\mu_0 K = 0.0002513$ T; outside they cancel, giving zero.

name: Far field of a small loop
statement: A small loop of radius $3.0$ cm carries $2.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field on the axis at $0.50$ m from the loop's center, in T.
solution: Use $B = \mu_0 I R^2/[2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}]$. Since $x \gg R$, this is nearly the dipole result $\mu_0\mu/(2\pi x^3)$. Numerically $B = 8.999e-09$ T.

name: Field at a square's corner
statement: A square loop of side $10$ cm carries $6.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at one corner of the square, in T.
solution: The two sides meeting at that corner are collinear with the field point, so $d\vec{s}\times\hat{r} = 0$ and they contribute nothing. Each of the two far sides is a segment at distance $a$ subtending angles $0$ to $45^\circ$: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\sin45^\circ$ each. Both point the same way, so $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I\sin45^\circ}{2\pi a} = 8.485e-06$ T.

name: Center of a finite solenoid
statement: A solenoid $30$ cm long and $2.0$ cm in radius has $2000$ turns per meter and carries $3.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the axis, in T.
solution: Stack on-axis loop fields: $B = \tfrac12\mu_0 nI(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$, which at the center becomes $B = \mu_0 nI\,L/\sqrt{L^2+4R^2}$. Numerically $B = 0.007474$ T, about $1\%$ below the infinite-solenoid value $\mu_0 nI$.

name: Coil pair, wrong spacing
statement: Two coaxial coils, each of $50$ turns and radius $10$ cm, carry $2.0$ A in the same sense. Their planes are $30$ cm apart. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the midpoint on the axis, in T.
solution: Each coil is $d/2 = 0.15$ m from the midpoint and contributes $\mu_0 NIR^2/[2(R^2+(d/2)^2)^{3/2}]$; the two add. So $B = 0.0002145$ T. (This spacing is not the Helmholtz condition $d = R$, so the field here is not especially uniform.)

name: Three wires, field at the centroid
statement: Three long parallel wires pass through the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $20$ cm, each carrying $10$ A out of the page. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field magnitude at the centroid of the triangle, in T.
solution: The centroid is the same distance $s/\sqrt3 = 0.1155$ m from each wire, so all three contributions have equal magnitude $1.73e-05$ T. Each field is perpendicular to its own radial line, so the three vectors are separated by $120^\circ$ and sum to zero. $B = 0$.

name: Null point between two wires
statement: Two long parallel wires are $0.30$ m apart and carry $8.0$ A and $2.0$ A in the same direction. Find the distance from the $8.0$ A wire to the point on the line joining them where the net field is zero, in m.
solution: With parallel currents the fields oppose only between the wires. Setting $\mu_0 I_1/(2\pi x) = \mu_0 I_2/[2\pi(d-x)]$ gives $8(0.30-x) = 2x$, so $x = 2.4/10 = 0.24$ m from the $8.0$ A wire.

name: Center of a hexagonal loop
statement: A regular hexagonal loop of side $10$ cm carries $4.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center, in T.
solution: Each side is a finite segment at apothem distance $a = s/(2\tan30^\circ)$ subtending $\pm30^\circ$. Summing six sides gives $B = \dfrac{6\mu_0 I\sin30^\circ\tan30^\circ}{\pi s} = 2.771e-05$ T, already close to the circular-loop value for the same perimeter.

name: Spinning charged ring
statement: A thin insulating ring of radius $10$ cm carries a uniformly distributed charge of $5.0\,\mu$C and spins about its axis at $20$ revolutions per second. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the ring, in T.
solution: A rotating ring of charge is a steady current $I = qf = (5.0\times10^{-6})(20) = 0.0001$ A, since the whole charge passes any point $f$ times per second. Then $B = \mu_0 I/(2R) = 6.283e-10$ T.

name: Spinning charged disk
statement: A flat insulating disk of radius $5.0$ cm carries a uniformly distributed surface charge totalling $2.0\,\mu$C and spins about its axis at $\omega = 100$ rad/s. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A. Find the field at the center of the disk, in T.
solution: Treat the disk as nested rings. A ring at radius $r$ of width $dr$ holds $dq = \sigma 2\pi r\,dr$ and rotates $\omega/2\pi$ times per second, so $dI = \sigma\omega r\,dr$ and $dB = \mu_0 dI/(2r) = \tfrac12\mu_0\sigma\omega\,dr$. Integrating from $0$ to $R$: $B = \mu_0\sigma\omega R/2$ with $\sigma = Q/(\pi R^2) = 0.0002546$ C/m$^2$, giving $B = 8e-10$ T.

name: Field beside a straight wire
statement: A long straight copper wire carries a steady current of $5.0$ A. Using $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A, find the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point $2.0$ cm from the wire's axis, in T.
solution: An Amperian circle of radius $r$ centered on the wire has $B$ constant and tangential, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I$. Then $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.0)}{2\pi(0.020)} = 5.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Ideal solenoid interior
statement: A long solenoid is wound with $1200$ turns per meter and carries $2.5$ A. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field on its axis, far from the ends, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: A rectangular Amperian loop with one side inside the solenoid and one side outside (where $B\approx 0$) gives $B\ell = \mu_0 (n\ell) I$. So $$B = \mu_0 n I = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(1200)(2.5) = 3.77\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Toroid on a ferrite-free core
statement: A toroidal coil of $500$ turns carries $3.0$ A. Find the magnitude of the field along the circle of radius $0.10$ m inside the windings, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: A circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ inside the toroid encloses all $N$ turns once each, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 N I$. Then $$B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(500)(3.0)}{2\pi(0.10)} = 3.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Inside a solid conductor
statement: A long cylindrical wire of radius $2.0$ mm carries $10$ A spread uniformly over its cross-section. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point $1.0$ mm from the axis, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Only the current inside radius $r$ counts: $I_{\text{enc}} = I r^2/R^2$. Then $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(10)(0.0010)}{2\pi(0.0020)^2} = 5.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Between the conductors of a coax
statement: A coaxial cable has a thin inner conductor carrying $4.0$ A and an outer shell carrying $4.0$ A in the opposite direction. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field in the gap, at radius $3.0$ mm from the axis, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: In the gap the Amperian circle encloses only the inner conductor, so the return current is irrelevant there. $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(4.0)}{2\pi(0.0030)} = 2.67\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Line integral around three wires
statement: A closed loop encircles three parallel wires. Two carry $8.0$ A and $5.0$ A out of the page; the third carries $3.0$ A into the page. Taking the loop counterclockwise, evaluate $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ in T·m. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: By the right-hand rule, currents out of the page are positive for a counterclockwise loop, so $I_{\text{enc}} = 8.0 + 5.0 - 3.0 = 10.0$ A. Then $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}} = 1.257\times10^{-5}\ \text{T·m}.$$

name: Solenoid from total turns
statement: A solenoid $0.50$ m long has $800$ turns and carries $1.5$ A. Treating it as ideal, find the field magnitude at its center, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.

name: Infinite sheet of current
statement: A large flat conducting sheet carries a uniform surface current density of $50$ A/m. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field just above the sheet, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Use a rectangular loop of length $L$ straddling the sheet. The field is parallel to the sheet, opposite on the two sides, so $2BL = \mu_0 K L$. Then $$B = \frac{\mu_0 K}{2} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(50)}{2} = 3.14\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Cavity of a hollow shell
statement: A long hollow cylindrical conductor has inner radius $3.0$ cm and outer radius $5.0$ cm and carries $12$ A distributed uniformly through its wall. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point $2.0$ cm from the axis, in T.
solution: An Amperian circle of radius $2.0$ cm lies entirely in the hollow region, so $I_{\text{enc}} = 0$ and $B(2\pi r) = 0$. The field in the cavity is exactly zero regardless of the shell's current.

name: Current needed for a target field
statement: A solenoid wound at $2000$ turns per meter must produce a $0.050$ T field inside. Find the required current, in A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.

name: Where the field is half its surface value
statement: A long wire of radius $5.0$ mm carries $20$ A uniformly distributed. Inside the wire, find the distance from the axis at which the field magnitude is half its value at the surface. Give the answer in mm.
solution: Inside, $B(r) = \mu_0 I r/(2\pi R^2)$ grows linearly with $r$, and $B(R) = \mu_0 I/(2\pi R)$. Half the surface value therefore occurs at $r = R/2 = 2.5$ mm.

name: Inside the braid of a coaxial cable
statement: A coax has a solid inner conductor of radius $1.0$ mm carrying $6.0$ A, and an outer shell from $3.0$ mm to $4.0$ mm carrying $6.0$ A in the opposite direction, uniformly across its cross-section. Find the magnitude of the field at radius $3.5$ mm, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: The Amperian circle encloses the full inner current plus the fraction of the return current lying inside $r$: $$I_{\text{enc}} = 6.0 - 6.0\,\frac{r^2-b^2}{c^2-b^2} = 6.0 - 6.0\frac{(3.5^2-3^2)}{(4^2-3^2)} = 3.21\ \text{A}.$$ Then $B = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}/(2\pi r) = 1.84\times10^{-4}$ T.

name: Inside a thick current slab
statement: A very wide conducting slab of thickness $4.0$ cm carries a uniform current density of $1.0\times10^{5}$ A/m² parallel to its faces. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point $1.0$ cm from the central plane, still inside the slab, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: By symmetry $B = 0$ on the central plane and is antisymmetric across it. A rectangular loop of length $L$ from $-x$ to $+x$ gives $2BL = \mu_0 J (2xL)$, so $$B = \mu_0 J x = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(10^{5})(0.010) = 1.26\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Outside the same slab
statement: The same wide slab of thickness $4.0$ cm carries a uniform current density $1.0\times10^{5}$ A/m². Find the magnitude of the field just outside one face, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Once the loop encloses the whole thickness $2d = 4.0$ cm, the enclosed current stops growing: $2BL = \mu_0 J (2dL)$, so $$B = \mu_0 J d = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(10^{5})(0.020) = 2.51\times10^{-3}\ \text{T},$$ constant everywhere outside.

name: Toroid field at the inner edge
statement: A toroid with $1200$ turns carries $2.0$ A. Its cross-section extends from inner radius $8.0$ cm to outer radius $12$ cm. Find the field magnitude at the inner edge, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Inside a toroid $B = \mu_0 N I/(2\pi r)$, which is strongest at the smallest radius. $$B = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1200)(2.0)}{2\pi(0.080)} = 6.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Two sheets carrying opposite currents
statement: Two large parallel sheets each carry a surface current density of $80$ A/m, in opposite directions. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field in the region between them, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Each sheet alone gives $\mu_0 K/2$. Between the sheets the two contributions point the same way and add; outside they cancel. So $$B = \mu_0 K = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(80) = 1.005\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Wire with current density growing outward
statement: A wire of radius $4.0$ mm carries a total current of $10$ A with a current density $J(r) = J_0 r/R$ that increases linearly with distance from the axis. Find the field magnitude at $r = 2.0$ mm, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Integrating, $I_{\text{enc}} = \int_0^r J_0 (r'/R) 2\pi r'\,dr' = 2\pi J_0 r^3/(3R)$, and setting $r=R$ gives $I = 2\pi J_0 R^2/3$. Hence $I_{\text{enc}} = I r^3/R^3$ and $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2\pi R^3} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(10)(0.0020)^2}{2\pi(0.0040)^3} = 1.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Two windings on one solenoid
statement: A long tube carries two windings: an inner layer of $1500$ turns per meter and an outer layer of $900$ turns per meter, each carrying $2.0$ A but wound in opposite senses. Find the field magnitude on the axis, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: An Amperian rectangle inside both layers encloses the net turn density, so the fields subtract: $$B = \mu_0 (n_1 I_1 - n_2 I_2) = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(3000-1800) = 1.51\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Halfway through a thick pipe
statement: A long pipe with inner radius $2.0$ cm and outer radius $6.0$ cm carries $30$ A uniformly through its wall. Find the field magnitude at $r = 4.0$ cm, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: The enclosed current is the fraction of wall area inside $r$: $$I_{\text{enc}} = I\frac{r^2-a^2}{b^2-a^2} = 30\frac{16-4}{36-4} = 11.25\ \text{A},$$ so $B = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}/(2\pi r) = 5.63\times10^{-5}$ T.

name: Circulation around solenoid turns
statement: A rectangular Amperian loop is drawn so that it links $250$ turns of a solenoid carrying $1.2$ A. Evaluate $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ around that loop, in T·m. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Each linked turn contributes its full current to $I_{\text{enc}}$, so $I_{\text{enc}} = 250(1.2) = 300$ A. Then $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 (300) = 3.77\times10^{-4}$ T·m, independent of the loop's shape.

name: Imperfectly shielded coax
statement: A coax's inner conductor carries $7.0$ A, but only $5.0$ A returns along the shield; the rest leaks away elsewhere. Find the field magnitude at $r = 8.0$ mm, outside the shield, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Outside, $I_{\text{enc}} = 7.0 - 5.0 = 2.0$ A, so the cable is no longer field-free outside. $$B = \frac{\mu_0(2.0)}{2\pi(0.0080)} = 5.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Designing a toroid
statement: A toroid of mean radius $0.15$ m is to produce $0.020$ T at that radius with a current of $4.0$ A. Find the number of turns required. Give a pure number (turns).

name: Uniform field inside a drilled cavity
statement: A long conductor carries uniform current density $2.0\times10^{6}$ A/m² out of the page. A cylindrical hole is bored parallel to the axis, its center offset $1.0$ cm from the conductor's axis. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field everywhere inside the hole, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Superpose a full cylinder of density $J$ with a cylinder of density $-J$ filling the hole. Inside a uniform cylinder $\vec{B} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 J \hat{z}\times\vec{r}$ measured from that cylinder's own axis, so the two contributions combine to $\vec{B} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 J \hat{z}\times\vec{d}$, a uniform field. Thus $$B = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 J d = \tfrac{1}{2}(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.0\times10^{6})(0.010) = 1.26\times10^{-2}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Density falling off toward the surface
statement: A wire of radius $6.0$ mm carries a total of $9.0$ A with current density $J(r) = J_0(1 - r/R)$. Find the field magnitude at $r = R/2 = 3.0$ mm, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: $I_{\text{enc}}(r) = 2\pi J_0\left(\frac{r^2}{2}-\frac{r^3}{3R}\right)$ and the total is $I = \pi J_0 R^2/3$. At $r=R/2$ the bracket gives $2\pi J_0 R^2/12 = \pi J_0 R^2/6 = I/2$, so exactly half the current is enclosed. Then $$B = \frac{\mu_0 (I/2)}{2\pi (R/2)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} = 3.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Slab with density growing from the midplane
statement: A wide slab occupies $-d \le y \le d$ with $d = 2.0$ cm and carries current density $J = J_0|y|/d$ with $J_0 = 4.0\times10^{5}$ A/m². Find the field magnitude at $y = d/2 = 1.0$ cm, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: The field vanishes at $y=0$ by symmetry, so a loop from $-y$ to $y$ gives $2B = \mu_0 \int_{-y}^{y} J\,dy' = \mu_0 J_0 y^2/d$. Hence $B = \mu_0 J_0 y^2/(2d)$, and at $y = d/2$, $$B = \frac{\mu_0 J_0 d}{8} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(4.0\times10^{5})(0.020)}{8} = 1.26\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Coax with currents in the same direction
statement: A miswired coaxial cable carries $10$ A along the inner conductor and $4.0$ A along the shield in the same direction. Find the field magnitude at $r = 5.0$ mm, outside both conductors, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Ampere's law cares only about the algebraic sum enclosed: $I_{\text{enc}} = 10 + 4.0 = 14$ A. Then $$B = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(14)}{2\pi(0.0050)} = 5.60\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$ With the currents antiparallel the field outside would instead be zero.

name: Wire balanced against a sheet
statement: A long straight wire carries $12$ A and a large flat sheet carries a surface current density of $30$ A/m. Find the distance from the wire at which the wire's field magnitude equals the sheet's field magnitude, in m.
solution: Set $\mu_0 I/(2\pi r) = \mu_0 K/2$. The permeability cancels, leaving $$r = \frac{I}{\pi K} = \frac{12}{\pi(30)} = 0.127\ \text{m}.$$

name: Flux through a toroid's cross-section
statement: A toroid of square cross-section has inner radius $0.10$ m, outer radius $0.14$ m, height $0.040$ m, $800$ turns, and carries $5.0$ A. Find the magnetic flux through one cross-section, in Wb. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: $B$ varies as $1/r$ across the cross-section, so integrate: $$\Phi = \int_a^b \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r} h\,dr = \frac{\mu_0 N I h}{2\pi}\ln\frac{b}{a} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(800)(5.0)(0.040)}{2\pi}\ln(1.4) = 1.08\times10^{-5}\ \text{Wb}.$$

name: Field at the axis of a drilled conductor
statement: A long conductor of radius $R = 1.0$ cm has a cylindrical hole of radius $R/2$ bored parallel to its axis, with the hole's axis passing through the point a distance $R/2$ from the conductor's axis. The remaining metal carries $15$ A uniformly. Find the field magnitude at the conductor's original axis, in T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Superpose a full cylinder of density $J$ with a $-J$ cylinder filling the hole. At the original axis the full cylinder contributes nothing. The negative cylinder's axis is $R/2$ away, which is exactly its own surface, so it contributes $B = \mu_0 J (R/2)/2 = \mu_0 J R/4$. The real current fixes $J$: $I = J\left(\pi R^2 - \pi R^2/4\right) = \tfrac{3}{4}\pi J R^2$, so $J = 4I/(3\pi R^2)$ and $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{3\pi R} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(15)}{3\pi(0.010)} = 2.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}.$$

name: Where the shield halves the field
statement: A coax carries $8.0$ A out along a thin inner wire and $8.0$ A back through a shield extending from $3.0$ mm to $5.0$ mm, uniformly distributed. Find the radius inside the shield at which the field magnitude has fallen to half its value at the shield's inner surface. Give the answer in mm.
solution: At $r=b=3.0$ mm, $B_b = \mu_0 I/(2\pi b) = 5.33\times10^{-4}$ T. Inside the shield $$B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\left(1 - \frac{r^2-b^2}{c^2-b^2}\right).$$ Setting $B(r) = B_b/2$ gives $\frac{b}{r}\left(1-\frac{r^2-b^2}{c^2-b^2}\right)=\tfrac12$; solving numerically on $3 < r < 5$ mm yields $r = 3.84$ mm.

name: Loop in a strengthening field
statement: A single flat loop of area $0.020$ m² sits perpendicular to a magnetic field that grows at $0.50$ T/s. Find the magnitude of the induced EMF, in V.
solution: With the area fixed, $|\varepsilon| = |d\Phi/dt| = A\,|dB/dt|$. So $\varepsilon = (0.020)(0.50) = 0.010$ V.

name: Many turns multiply the EMF
statement: A coil of $200$ turns, each of area $0.0050$ m², lies perpendicular to a field changing at $1.2$ T/s. Find the magnitude of the induced EMF, in V.
solution: Each turn sees the same flux change, so $|\varepsilon| = N A |dB/dt| = (200)(0.0050)(1.2) = 1.2$ V.

name: Rod sliding on rails
statement: A copper rod $0.25$ m long slides at $4.0$ m/s along horizontal rails in a vertical magnetic field of $0.30$ T. Find the magnitude of the motional EMF, in V.
solution: The circuit area grows at $L v$, so $|\varepsilon| = B L v = (0.30)(0.25)(4.0) = 0.30$ V.

name: Flux change in a short time
statement: The flux through a single loop changes by $0.060$ Wb in $0.020$ s at a steady rate. Find the magnitude of the average induced EMF, in V.
solution: $|\varepsilon| = |\Delta\Phi|/\Delta t = 0.060/0.020 = 3.0$ V.

name: Induced current from an EMF
statement: An induced EMF of $1.5$ V drives current around a closed loop of total resistance $3.0$ $\Omega$. Find the magnitude of the induced current, in A.
solution: The loop obeys Ohm's law with the induced EMF as the source: $I = \varepsilon/R = 1.5/3.0 = 0.50$ A.

name: Collapsing loop
statement: A flexible loop in a steady $0.80$ T field perpendicular to its plane is squeezed so its area drops from $0.040$ m² to $0.010$ m² in $0.50$ s. Find the magnitude of the average induced EMF, in V.
solution: Here $B$ is fixed and $A$ changes: $|\varepsilon| = B|\Delta A|/\Delta t = (0.80)(0.030)/(0.50) = 0.048$ V.

name: Charge through a coil
statement: A $50$-turn coil in a circuit of resistance $10$ $\Omega$ has its flux per turn changed by $0.0040$ Wb. Find the total charge that flows through the coil, in C.
solution: Integrating $I = N|d\Phi/dt|/R$ over time gives $$q = \frac{N|\Delta\Phi|}{R} = \frac{(50)(0.0040)}{10} = 0.020\ \text{C},$$ independent of how fast the change happens.

name: Flux through a circular loop
statement: A circular loop of radius $0.10$ m lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform $0.40$ T field. Find the magnetic flux through the loop, in Wb.

name: Peak EMF of a generator coil
statement: A generator coil of $100$ turns, each of area $0.020$ m², spins at $60$ rad/s in a $0.25$ T field about an axis perpendicular to the field. Find the peak EMF, in V.
solution: The flux is $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, so $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$ and the peak is $$\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega = (100)(0.25)(0.020)(60) = 30\ \text{V}.$$

name: Power in the sliding rod circuit
statement: A sliding rod produces a motional EMF of $0.30$ V in a circuit whose total resistance is $0.15$ $\Omega$. Find the power dissipated, in W.
solution: $P = \varepsilon^2/R = (0.30)^2/0.15 = 0.60$ W. This equals the mechanical power the puller must supply.

name: Force needed to keep a rod moving
statement: A rod of length $0.30$ m slides at a constant $6.0$ m/s on frictionless rails in a $0.40$ T perpendicular field; the circuit resistance is $0.50$ $\Omega$. Find the magnitude of the applied force needed, in N.
solution: The induced current $I = BLv/R$ feels a force $BIL$ opposing the motion (Lenz), so the applied force must match it: $$F = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R} = \frac{(0.40)^2(0.30)^2(6.0)}{0.50} = 0.173\ \text{N}.$$

name: Charge as a loop leaves the field
statement: A square loop of side $0.20$ m and resistance $2.0$ $\Omega$ is pulled completely out of a $0.35$ T perpendicular field. Find the total charge that flows, in C.
solution: The flux goes from $BA$ to zero, so $$q = \frac{|\Delta\Phi|}{R} = \frac{(0.35)(0.20)^2}{2.0} = 7.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{C},$$ regardless of how fast it is pulled.

name: RMS output of an alternator
statement: An alternator coil has $150$ turns of area $0.015$ m² and spins at $50$ Hz in a $0.30$ T field. Find the RMS EMF, in V.
solution: Peak EMF is $NBA\omega$ with $\omega = 2\pi(50) = 314$ rad/s, giving $212.1$ V. The RMS value is $$\varepsilon_{\text{rms}} = \frac{NBA\omega}{\sqrt{2}} = 149.9\ \text{V}.$$

name: Loop beside a wire with rising current
statement: A rectangular loop with sides $0.30$ m long parallel to a straight wire has its near edge $2.0$ cm from the wire and its far edge $8.0$ cm from the wire. The wire's current increases at $200$ A/s. Find the magnitude of the induced EMF, in V. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: The wire's field falls off as $1/r$, so $$\Phi = \int_d^{d+w}\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\ell\,dr = \frac{\mu_0 I \ell}{2\pi}\ln\frac{d+w}{d}.$$ Then $|\varepsilon| = \frac{\mu_0 \ell}{2\pi}\ln(4)\,\frac{dI}{dt} = 1.66\times10^{-5}$ V.

name: Pickup coil around a solenoid
statement: A long solenoid of radius $1.0$ cm with $2500$ turns per meter has its current ramped at $40$ A/s. An $80$-turn pickup coil is wound tightly around it. Find the magnitude of the EMF induced in the pickup coil, in V. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Only the solenoid's interior carries flux, so each pickup turn links $\Phi = \mu_0 n I \pi r^2$. Thus $$|\varepsilon| = N\mu_0 n \pi r^2 \frac{dI}{dt} = (80)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2500)\pi(0.010)^2(40) = 3.16\times10^{-3}\ \text{V}.$$

name: Flipping a coil over
statement: A $120$-turn coil of area $0.0040$ m² sits perpendicular to a $0.25$ T field and is flipped through $180^\circ$. The circuit resistance is $8.0$ $\Omega$. Find the total charge that flows, in C.
solution: The flux per turn reverses sign, so $|\Delta\Phi| = 2BA$, not $BA$ — this factor of two is the whole point of a flip coil. $$q = \frac{2NBA}{R} = \frac{2(120)(0.25)(0.0040)}{8.0} = 0.030\ \text{C}.$$

name: Current in a loop in a decaying field
statement: A single circular loop of radius $4.0$ cm and resistance $2.5$ $\Omega$ lies perpendicular to a field that is decreasing at $0.60$ T/s. Find the magnitude of the induced current, in A.
solution: By Lenz's law the induced current flows so as to maintain the dying flux, i.e. in the same sense as the original field, but its magnitude is $$I = \frac{A|dB/dt|}{R} = \frac{\pi(0.040)^2(0.60)}{2.5} = 1.21\times10^{-3}\ \text{A}.$$

name: Loop being pulled tight
statement: A circular loop of radius $8.0$ cm lies in a uniform $0.60$ T field perpendicular to its plane. Its radius is shrinking at $0.020$ m/s. Find the magnitude of the induced EMF at that instant, in V.
solution: With $A = \pi r^2$, $dA/dt = 2\pi r\,dr/dt$, so $$|\varepsilon| = B\,2\pi r\left|\frac{dr}{dt}\right| = (0.60)(2\pi)(0.080)(0.020) = 6.03\times10^{-3}\ \text{V}.$$

name: Work to drag a loop out
statement: A square loop of side $0.20$ m and resistance $0.40$ $\Omega$ is pulled at a constant $3.0$ m/s out of a $0.50$ T field region. Find the total energy dissipated in the loop while it leaves the field, in J.
solution: While only one side is in the field, the retarding force is $F = B^2L^2v/R = 0.075$ N, and the loop travels $L = 0.20$ m before clearing the boundary. Then $$W = F L = (0.075)(0.20) = 0.015\ \text{J},$$ all of it appearing as resistive heat.

name: Terminal speed of a falling loop
statement: A square loop of side $0.25$ m, mass $20$ g, and resistance $0.60$ $\Omega$ falls with its lower edge crossing the boundary of a horizontal $0.50$ T field region. Using $g = 9.8$ m/s², find its terminal speed, in m/s.
solution: At terminal speed the magnetic drag balances gravity: $B^2L^2v/R = mg$, so $$v = \frac{mgR}{B^2L^2} = \frac{(0.020)(9.8)(0.60)}{(0.50)^2(0.25)^2} = 7.53\ \text{m/s}.$$

name: Heat from a quenched field
statement: A $40$-turn coil of radius $5.0$ cm and total resistance $1.2$ $\Omega$ sits perpendicular to a field that drops steadily from $0.20$ T to zero in $0.10$ s. Find the energy dissipated in the coil, in J.
solution: The EMF is constant: $\varepsilon = N\pi r^2 \Delta B/\Delta t = (40)\pi(0.050)^2(2.0) = 0.628$ V. Then $$Q = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{R}\Delta t = \frac{(0.628)^2}{1.2}(0.10) = 0.0329\ \text{J}.$$

name: Faraday disk
statement: A copper disk of radius $0.15$ m spins at $120$ rad/s about its axis in a $0.40$ T field parallel to the axis. Find the EMF between the axle and the rim, in V.
solution: A radial element at $r$ moves at $\omega r$, contributing $B\omega r\,dr$. Integrating, $$\varepsilon = \int_0^R B\omega r\,dr = \tfrac12 B\omega R^2 = \tfrac12(0.40)(120)(0.15)^2 = 0.54\ \text{V}.$$

name: Induced current beside a ramping wire
statement: A rectangular loop of resistance $0.020$ $\Omega$ has sides of length $0.20$ m parallel to a long straight wire, at distances $1.0$ cm and $5.0$ cm from it. The wire's current rises at $500$ A/s. Find the magnitude of the induced current in the loop, in A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: The flux is $\Phi = \frac{\mu_0 I \ell}{2\pi}\ln(d_2/d_1)$, so $$|\varepsilon| = \frac{\mu_0 \ell \ln 5}{2\pi}\frac{dI}{dt} = 3.22\times10^{-5}\ \text{V}.$$ Then $I = \varepsilon/R = 1.61\times10^{-3}$ A. By Lenz's law it circulates opposite to the wire's current as seen through the loop.

name: Rod coasting to a stop
statement: A rod of mass $30$ g and length $0.40$ m slides freely on frictionless rails in a $0.60$ T perpendicular field with circuit resistance $0.80$ $\Omega$. It is released at $2.0$ m/s with no applied force. Find its speed $0.50$ s later, in m/s.
solution: The only horizontal force is the magnetic drag: $m\,dv/dt = -B^2L^2v/R$, so $v(t) = v_0 e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = mR/(B^2L^2) = (0.030)(0.80)/[(0.60)^2(0.40)^2] = 0.4167$ s. Then $v = 2.0\,e^{-1.20} = 0.602$ m/s.

name: Loop drifting away from a wire
statement: A rectangular loop with sides $0.40$ m parallel to a long wire carrying a steady $15$ A moves directly away from the wire at $2.5$ m/s. At the instant its near edge is $5.0$ cm and its far edge is $13$ cm from the wire, find the magnitude of the induced EMF, in V. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Treat each long side as a moving rod: $\varepsilon = B_1\ell v - B_2\ell v$ with $B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$. So $$|\varepsilon| = \frac{\mu_0 I \ell v}{2\pi}\left(\frac{1}{d_1}-\frac{1}{d_2}\right) = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(15)(0.40)(2.5)}{2\pi}\left(20 - 7.692\right) = 3.69\times10^{-5}\ \text{V}.$$

name: Charge from repositioning a loop
statement: A rectangular loop $0.40$ m long and $0.080$ m wide, of resistance $0.25$ $\Omega$, lies beside a wire carrying a steady $15$ A with its near edge $5.0$ cm away. It is moved until the near edge is $10$ cm away. Find the total charge that flows, in C. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: With $\Phi(d) = \frac{\mu_0 I \ell}{2\pi}\ln\frac{d+w}{d}$, $$q = \frac{|\Delta\Phi|}{R} = \frac{\mu_0 I \ell}{2\pi R}\left[\ln\frac{0.13}{0.05}-\ln\frac{0.18}{0.10}\right] = 1.77\times10^{-6}\ \text{C}.$$ Speed and path do not matter.

name: Induced electric field inside a solenoid
statement: Inside a long solenoid of radius $6.0$ cm the field is uniform and increasing at $0.80$ T/s. Find the magnitude of the induced electric field at a point $3.0$ cm from the axis, in V/m.
solution: Faraday's law in the form $\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -d\Phi/dt$ on a circle of radius $r$ gives $E(2\pi r) = \pi r^2\,dB/dt$, so $$E = \frac{r}{2}\frac{dB}{dt} = \frac{0.030}{2}(0.80) = 0.012\ \text{V/m}.$$ No conductor is needed; the field exists in empty space.

name: Induced electric field outside the windings
statement: For the same solenoid of radius $6.0$ cm with $dB/dt = 0.80$ T/s, find the magnitude of the induced electric field at $10$ cm from the axis, outside the windings, in V/m.
solution: Outside, the enclosed flux stops growing with $r$: $E(2\pi r) = \pi R^2 dB/dt$, so $$E = \frac{R^2}{2r}\frac{dB}{dt} = \frac{(0.060)^2}{2(0.10)}(0.80) = 0.0144\ \text{V/m}.$$ Note $E\ne 0$ even where $B = 0$.

name: Heat from a loop falling at terminal speed
statement: A conducting loop of mass $50$ g falls at its terminal speed through a horizontal field boundary, descending $0.80$ m while the drag force acts. Using $g = 9.8$ m/s², find the energy dissipated in the loop's resistance, in J.
solution: At terminal speed the kinetic energy never changes, so every joule of gravitational potential energy released must go into resistive heat: $$Q = mgh = (0.050)(9.8)(0.80) = 0.392\ \text{J}.$$ Neither $B$, $L$, nor $R$ is needed — they only set the speed, not the energy budget.

name: Small loop at the center of a big one
statement: A small loop of radius $2.0$ cm lies flat at the center of a coplanar large loop of radius $0.20$ m, both single turns. The large loop's current changes at $3000$ A/s. Find the magnitude of the EMF induced in the small loop, in V. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A.
solution: Because the small loop is tiny, the big loop's central field $B = \mu_0 I/(2R)$ is essentially uniform over it, so $\Phi = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\pi r^2$. Then $$|\varepsilon| = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2R}\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})\pi(0.020)^2}{2(0.20)}(3000) = 1.18\times10^{-5}\ \text{V}.$$

name: Rod on rails
statement: A copper rod of length $0.50$ m slides along horizontal rails at $3.0$ m/s. A uniform magnetic field of $0.40$ T points vertically, perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Find the EMF induced across the rod in volts.
solution: A rod moving perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ develops $\varepsilon = BLv$. So $\varepsilon = (0.40)(0.50)(3.0) = 0.60$ V.

name: Speed from a measured EMF
statement: A rod of length $0.25$ m slides on rails in a perpendicular field of $0.80$ T. A voltmeter across the rails reads $1.2$ V. Find the speed of the rod in m/s.
solution: Invert $\varepsilon = BLv$: $v = \varepsilon/(BL) = 1.2/[(0.80)(0.25)] = 6.0$ m/s.

name: Current in the rail loop
statement: A rod of length $0.40$ m slides at $5.0$ m/s on frictionless rails in a perpendicular field of $0.25$ T. The rails are joined by a $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor; all other resistance is negligible. Find the current in the loop in amperes.
solution: The rod acts as a battery of EMF $\varepsilon = BLv = (0.25)(0.40)(5.0) = 0.50$ V. Then $I = \varepsilon/R = 0.50/2.0 = 0.25$ A.

name: Force needed to keep the rod moving
statement: A rod of length $0.60$ m is pulled at a constant $4.0$ m/s along frictionless rails closed by a $1.5\ \Omega$ resistor. The perpendicular field is $0.30$ T. Find the magnitude of the applied force in newtons.
solution: The induced current $I = BLv/R$ feels a retarding force $F = BIL = B^2L^2v/R$. At constant speed the applied force matches it: $F = (0.30)^2(0.60)^2(4.0)/1.5 = 0.0864$ N.

name: Power dissipated in the rail circuit
statement: A conducting rod ($L = 0.60$ m) slides at $v = 4.0$ m/s along frictionless rails in a $B = 0.30$ T field perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The rails are closed by a $R = 1.5\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the power dissipated in the resistor in watts.
solution: $\varepsilon = BLv = 0.72$ V, so $P = \varepsilon^2/R = (0.72)^2/1.5 = 0.3456$ W. This equals the mechanical power $Fv$ supplied by the puller.

name: Rotating rod
statement: A straight rod of length $0.30$ m rotates about one end at $20$ rad/s in a uniform $0.50$ T field parallel to the rotation axis. Find the EMF between the ends of the rod in volts.
solution: Each element $dr$ at radius $r$ contributes $B\omega r\,dr$, so $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega L^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.50)(20)(0.30)^2 = 0.450$ V.

name: AC generator peak EMF
statement: A generator coil has $200$ turns, area $0.020$ m$^2$, and spins at $120$ rad/s in a uniform $0.10$ T field. Find the peak EMF in volts.
solution: For a coil rotating in a uniform field, $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$, so the peak is $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega = (200)(0.10)(0.020)(120) = 48.0$ V.

name: EMF across an airplane wing
statement: A jet with a $35$ m wingspan flies horizontally at $250$ m/s where the vertical component of Earth's field is $5.0\times10^{-5}$ T. Find the EMF between the wingtips in volts.
solution: Only the field component perpendicular to both the wing and the velocity matters, which is the vertical component. $\varepsilon = B_\perp L v = (5.0\times10^{-5})(35)(250) = 0.4375$ V.

name: Disk dynamo EMF
statement: A metal disk of radius $0.10$ m spins at $30$ revolutions per second about its axis in a $0.20$ T field parallel to the axis. Brushes contact the axle and the rim. Find the EMF between axle and rim in volts.
solution: A radius of the disk is a rotating rod: $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega R^2$ with $\omega = 2\pi(30) = 188.5$ rad/s. So $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}(0.20)(188.5)(0.10)^2 = 0.1885$ V.

name: Charge through the rail circuit
statement: A rod of length $0.20$ m slides $0.50$ m along rails in a perpendicular $0.40$ T field. The circuit has total resistance $0.10\ \Omega$. Find the total charge that flows in coulombs.
solution: Charge does not depend on how fast the rod moves: $q = \int I\,dt = \Delta\Phi/R$. Here $\Delta\Phi = BL d = (0.40)(0.20)(0.50) = 0.040$ Wb, so $q = 0.040/0.10 = 0.40$ C.

name: Terminal speed on inclined rails
statement: Frictionless rails $0.30$ m apart lie on a plane inclined at $30^\circ$. A $0.050$ kg rod slides down them; a $0.40\ \Omega$ resistor closes the circuit. A uniform $0.50$ T field points perpendicular to the inclined plane. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the terminal speed in m/s.
solution: At terminal speed the magnetic force balances the component of gravity along the incline: $B^2L^2v/R = mg\sin\theta$. So $v = mgR\sin\theta/(B^2L^2) = (0.050)(9.8)(0.40)(0.5)/[(0.50)^2(0.30)^2] = 4.356$ m/s.

name: Falling wire between vertical rails
statement: A $0.020$ kg wire of length $0.25$ m slides without friction down two vertical rails joined at the top by a $0.30\ \Omega$ resistor. A horizontal $0.60$ T field is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the terminal speed in m/s.

name: Magnetic braking: time to half speed
statement: A $0.10$ kg rod glides on frictionless rails ($L = 0.50$ m) closed by a $0.20\ \Omega$ resistor, in a perpendicular $0.80$ T field. It is released with some initial speed and slows only because of induction. Find the time for its speed to drop to half its initial value, in seconds.
solution: Newton's law gives $m\,dv/dt = -B^2L^2v/R$, so $v = v_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = mR/(B^2L^2) = 0.1250$ s. Half speed takes $t = \tau\ln 2 = 0.0866$ s.

name: Total sliding distance while braking
statement: The same rod ($m = 0.10$ kg, $L = 0.50$ m, $R = 0.20\ \Omega$, $B = 0.80$ T) starts at $6.0$ m/s. Find the total distance it travels before stopping, in meters.
solution: Since $v = v_0e^{-t/\tau}$, the total distance is $\int_0^\infty v\,dt = v_0\tau$ with $\tau = mR/(B^2L^2) = 0.1250$ s. So $d = (6.0)(0.1250) = 0.750$ m.

name: Heat generated by magnetic braking
statement: The same rod ($m = 0.10$ kg) starts at $6.0$ m/s and is brought to rest entirely by induction. Find the total heat dissipated in the resistor in joules.
solution: No other force does work, so all the kinetic energy ends up as resistive heat: $Q = \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.10)(6.0)^2 = 1.80$ J. The field values do not matter for the total, only for the rate.

name: Generator peak EMF from rpm
statement: A $50$-turn coil of area $0.040$ m$^2$ spins at $1500$ rpm in a uniform $0.25$ T field, with the rotation axis perpendicular to the field. Find the peak EMF in volts.

name: RMS output of the generator
statement: A $50$-turn coil of area $0.040$ m$^2$ spins at $1500$ rpm in a uniform $0.25$ T field, with the rotation axis perpendicular to the field. The generator produces a sinusoidal EMF. Find its rms value in volts.
solution: For a sinusoid, $\varepsilon_{\rm rms} = \varepsilon_0/\sqrt{2}$. With $\varepsilon_0 = 78.54$ V, $\varepsilon_{\rm rms} = 55.54$ V.

name: Spin rate for a target EMF
statement: A $0.50$ m rod pivots about one end in a uniform $0.40$ T field parallel to the axis. Find the angular speed, in rad/s, needed to produce $1.5$ V between the ends.
solution: Solve $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega L^2$ for $\omega$: $\omega = 2\varepsilon/(BL^2) = 2(1.5)/[(0.40)(0.50)^2] = 30.0$ rad/s.

name: Disk dynamo current
statement: A disk of radius $0.20$ m spins at $50$ rad/s in a $0.50$ T axial field. Brushes at the axle and rim connect to an external circuit of total resistance $0.050\ \Omega$. Find the current in amperes.
solution: The dynamo EMF is $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega R^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.50)(50)(0.20)^2 = 0.50$ V. Then $I = \varepsilon/R_{\rm ext} = 0.50/0.050 = 10.0$ A.

name: Charge with rod resistance included
statement: A rod of resistance $0.050\ \Omega$ and length $0.25$ m slides $1.2$ m along rails in a perpendicular $0.30$ T field. The rails are closed by a galvanometer of resistance $0.15\ \Omega$. Find the charge that passes through the galvanometer in coulombs.
solution: Total circuit resistance is $0.050 + 0.15 = 0.20\ \Omega$. The flux change is $\Delta\Phi = BLd = (0.30)(0.25)(1.2) = 0.090$ Wb, so $q = \Delta\Phi/R = 0.090/0.20 = 0.45$ C.

name: Rod pulled by a hanging mass
statement: A rod on horizontal frictionless rails $0.35$ m apart is pulled by a string over a pulley attached to a hanging $0.20$ kg block. The rails are closed by a $0.60\ \Omega$ resistor and the field is $0.70$ T perpendicular to the rail plane. The rod and string have negligible mass. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the terminal speed in m/s.
solution: With massless rod and string, terminal motion needs the magnetic force to balance the weight: $B^2L^2v/R = mg$. So $v = mgR/(B^2L^2) = (0.20)(9.8)(0.60)/[(0.70)^2(0.35)^2] = 19.59$ m/s.

name: Average power from an AC generator
statement: A $100$-turn coil of area $0.010$ m$^2$ rotates at $100$ rad/s in a $0.20$ T field and feeds a $5.0\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the average power delivered in watts.
solution: The peak EMF is $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega = (100)(0.20)(0.010)(100) = 20.0$ V. Averaging $\varepsilon^2/R$ over a cycle gives $P_{\rm avg} = \varepsilon_0^2/(2R) = 40.0$ W.

name: Pulling against friction and induction
statement: A rod of length $0.40$ m is dragged at a steady $3.0$ m/s along rails closed by a $0.80\ \Omega$ resistor, in a perpendicular $0.50$ T field. Friction adds a constant $0.050$ N of resistance. Find the total mechanical power the puller must supply in watts.
solution: The magnetic drag is $B^2L^2v/R = 0.150$ N; adding friction gives a total applied force of $0.200$ N. The power is $P = Fv = 0.600$ W, of which only the magnetic part becomes electrical energy.

name: Speed when acceleration is half of g
statement: A $0.030$ kg rod falls from rest along vertical rails $0.40$ m apart, with a horizontal $0.50$ T field perpendicular to the rail plane and a $0.25\ \Omega$ resistor closing the circuit. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the speed at which its acceleration has fallen to $g/2$, in m/s.
solution: Newton's law: $ma = mg - B^2L^2v/R$. Setting $a = g/2$ means the magnetic force equals $mg/2$, i.e. $v$ is half the terminal speed $v_T = mgR/(B^2L^2) = 1.8375$ m/s. So $v = 0.9187$ m/s.

name: Power from a rotating rod
statement: A rod of length $0.25$ m rotates at $40$ rad/s about one end, with its far end sliding on a circular rail. A uniform $0.60$ T field is parallel to the rotation axis and the circuit resistance is $1.5\ \Omega$. Find the electrical power generated in watts.
solution: The rotating rod gives $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega L^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.60)(40)(0.25)^2 = 0.750$ V, so $P = \varepsilon^2/R = 0.3750$ W. An external torque must supply exactly this power.

name: Rod on rails with a capacitor
statement: A $0.20$ kg rod of length $0.50$ m rides on frictionless rails closed by a $0.050$ F capacitor (no resistance anywhere). A perpendicular $0.80$ T field fills the region. A constant $0.50$ N force is applied. Find the acceleration of the rod in m/s$^2$.
solution: The capacitor charge is $q = C\varepsilon = CBLv$, so the current is $I = CBL\,a$ and the magnetic reaction force is $BIL = CB^2L^2a$. Then $F = (m + CB^2L^2)a$, giving $a = 0.50/(0.20 + 0.0080) = 2.404$ m/s$^2$: the capacitor acts like extra inertia.

name: Inclined rails with friction
statement: A $0.10$ kg rod slides down rails $0.40$ m apart on a $30^\circ$ incline, with coefficient of kinetic friction $0.10$ between rod and rails. The circuit resistance is $0.50\ \Omega$ and a $0.60$ T field is perpendicular to the inclined plane. Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the terminal speed in m/s.
solution: At terminal speed $mg\sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta = B^2L^2v/R$. The net driving force is $0.4051$ N, so $v = (0.4051)(0.50)/[(0.60)^2(0.40)^2] = 3.517$ m/s.

name: Charge from the impulse-momentum theorem
statement: A $0.050$ kg rod of length $0.50$ m is launched at $4.0$ m/s along frictionless rails in a perpendicular $0.40$ T field and coasts to rest through induction alone. Find the total charge that circulates, in coulombs.
solution: The retarding force is $BIL$, so $m\,dv = -BL\,I\,dt$ and integrating gives $mv_0 = BLq$. Thus $q = mv_0/(BL) = (0.050)(4.0)/[(0.40)(0.50)] = 1.00$ C, independent of the resistance.

name: Two free rods on the same rails
statement: Two identical rods, each of mass $0.10$ kg, rest on the same pair of frictionless rails in a uniform perpendicular field. One is given a speed of $5.0$ m/s toward the other; the rails and rods form a closed resistive circuit. Find the total heat dissipated by the time the motion settles, in joules.
solution: The two rods exert equal and opposite magnetic forces, so total momentum is conserved and current stops only when their velocities match, at $v_0/2$. Heat is the lost kinetic energy: $Q = \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 - \frac{1}{2}(2m)(v_0/2)^2 = \frac{1}{4}mv_0^2 = 0.6250$ J.

name: Rod on rails closed by an inductor
statement: A $0.10$ kg rod of length $0.40$ m slides on frictionless, resistanceless rails closed by a $0.50$ H inductor, in a perpendicular $0.60$ T field. The rod is given an initial speed of $2.0$ m/s. Find the maximum distance it travels from its starting point, in meters.
solution: With no resistance, $L\,dI/dt = BLv$ gives $I = (B\ell/L)x$, so the magnetic force $-B^2\ell^2x/L$ is a Hooke's-law restoring force. The motion is SHM with $\omega = B\ell/\sqrt{mL} = 1.0733$ rad/s, and the amplitude is $x_{\max} = v_0/\omega = 1.863$ m.

name: Inductance of a solenoid
statement: A solenoid has $500$ turns wound over a length of $0.25$ m, with cross-sectional area $4.0\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find its self-inductance in henries.

name: Self-induced EMF
statement: The current in a $0.15$ H inductor increases at a steady $40$ A/s. Find the magnitude of the self-induced EMF in volts.
solution: $|\varepsilon| = L\,|dI/dt| = (0.15)(40) = 6.0$ V, and by Lenz's law it opposes the increase.

name: Energy stored in an inductor
statement: A $0.20$ H inductor carries a steady current of $3.0$ A. Find the energy stored in its magnetic field in joules.

name: Magnetic energy density
statement: A region contains a uniform magnetic field of $0.80$ T. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find the magnetic energy density in J/m$^3$.

name: Mutual inductance EMF
statement: Two coils have a mutual inductance of $0.020$ H. The current in the first coil changes at $150$ A/s. Find the magnitude of the EMF induced in the second coil in volts.

name: LR time constant
statement: A $0.40$ H inductor is in series with a $25\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the time constant of the circuit in seconds.

name: Final current in an LR circuit
statement: A $12$ V battery is connected in series with a $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor and an ideal inductor. Find the steady current a long time after the switch closes, in amperes.
solution: Once the current stops changing, the inductor has no EMF and behaves like a wire: $I = V/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0$ A.

name: LC oscillation frequency
statement: A $2.0$ mH inductor is connected to a $5.0\ \mu$F capacitor. Find the natural oscillation frequency in hertz.

name: Inductors in series
statement: A $0.30$ H and a $0.50$ H inductor are connected in series, far enough apart that their mutual inductance is negligible. Find the equivalent inductance in henries.
solution: Series inductors share the same $dI/dt$ and their EMFs add: $L_{\rm eq} = L_1 + L_2 = 0.8$ H.

name: Inductors in parallel
statement: A $0.30$ H and a $0.60$ H inductor are connected in parallel with negligible mutual inductance. Find the equivalent inductance in henries.
solution: Parallel inductors share the same EMF, so $1/L_{\rm eq} = 1/L_1 + 1/L_2$, giving $L_{\rm eq} = (0.30)(0.60)/0.90 = 0.20$ H.

name: Inductance of a toroid
statement: A toroid of rectangular cross-section has $800$ turns, inner radius $0.050$ m, outer radius $0.080$ m, and height $0.020$ m. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find its self-inductance in henries.
solution: Inside a toroid $B = \mu_0NI/(2\pi r)$, so $\Phi = \int_a^b \frac{\mu_0NIh}{2\pi r}dr = \frac{\mu_0NIh}{2\pi}\ln(b/a)$ and $L = N\Phi/I = \frac{\mu_0N^2h}{2\pi}\ln(b/a) = 1.2032e-03$ H.

name: Flux linkage
statement: A $0.25$ H coil carries $4.0$ A. Find the total flux linkage $N\Phi$ through the coil in webers.
solution: Self-inductance is defined by $N\Phi = LI$, so $N\Phi = (0.25)(4.0) = 1.0$ Wb.

name: Current partway through the rise
statement: A $9.0$ V battery, a $3.0\ \Omega$ resistor and a $0.60$ H inductor are connected in series and the switch is closed at $t = 0$. Find the current at $t = 0.10$ s, in amperes.

name: Decay to a tenth of the initial current
statement: A $0.50$ H inductor carrying a steady current is suddenly switched into a closed loop with a $20\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the time for the current to fall to $10\%$ of its initial value, in seconds.
solution: The decay is $I = I_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = L/R = 0.025$ s. Setting $I/I_0 = 0.10$ gives $t = \tau\ln 10 = 0.0576$ s.

name: Stored energy at steady state
statement: A $24$ V battery drives a series circuit with a $12\ \Omega$ resistor and a $0.80$ H inductor. Find the energy stored in the inductor long after the switch closes, in joules.
solution: The final current is $I = V/R = 2.0$ A, so $U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.80)(2.0)^2 = 1.6$ J.

name: Solenoid energy from energy density
statement: A solenoid $0.40$ m long has $2000$ turns per meter, cross-sectional area $1.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$, and carries $5.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find the total magnetic energy stored in joules.
solution: Inside, $B = \mu_0nI = 0.01257$ T, so $u = B^2/(2\mu_0) = 62.83$ J/m$^3$. Multiplying by the volume $A\ell = 4.0\times10^{-4}$ m$^3$ gives $U = 2.5133e-02$ J.

name: Mutual inductance of a coil on a solenoid
statement: A solenoid of $400$ turns, length $0.30$ m and cross-sectional area $5.0\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$ has a short $50$-turn coil wound tightly around its middle. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find the mutual inductance in henries.
solution: Current $I$ in the solenoid makes $B = \mu_0N_1I/\ell$, so the outer coil links $N_2BA$. Then $M = \mu_0N_1N_2A/\ell = 4.1888e-05$ H.

name: Peak current in an LC circuit
statement: A $10$ mH inductor is connected to a $2.0\ \mu$F capacitor carrying a maximum charge of $4.0\times10^{-5}$ C. Find the maximum current in the circuit in amperes.
solution: The charge oscillates as $q = Q\cos(\omega t)$ with $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 7071.1$ rad/s, so $I_{\max} = \omega Q = 0.2828$ A.

name: Energy exchange in an LC circuit
statement: A $5.0\ \mu$F capacitor charged to $12$ V is connected across an $8.0$ mH inductor. Find the maximum current that flows, in amperes.
solution: All the electric energy converts to magnetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{1}{2}LI_{\max}^2$, so $I_{\max} = V\sqrt{C/L} = 12\sqrt{(5.0\times10^{-6})/(8.0\times10^{-3})} = 0.300$ A.

name: Back-EMF of a motor
statement: A DC motor connected to a $120$ V supply has armature resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ and draws $5.0$ A while running. Find the back-EMF in volts.
solution: The loop rule gives $V = \varepsilon_{\rm back} + IR$, so $\varepsilon_{\rm back} = 120 - (5.0)(2.0) = 110.0$ V. The remaining $IR$ term is the heat lost in the windings.

name: Initial rate of current rise
statement: A $15$ V battery is switched into a series circuit containing a $50$ mH inductor and a resistor. Find the initial rate of change of the current, in A/s.
solution: At $t = 0$ the current is zero, so the resistor drops nothing and the whole battery voltage appears across the inductor: $dI/dt = V/L = 15/0.050 = 300$ A/s. The resistance does not matter at this instant.

name: Period of an LC oscillator
statement: A $0.25$ H inductor and a $1.0\ \mu$F capacitor form a closed loop with negligible resistance. Find the period of oscillation in seconds.

name: Time to store half the final energy
statement: A $0.40$ H inductor and an $8.0\ \Omega$ resistor are switched across a battery at $t = 0$. Find the time at which the inductor stores half of its eventual energy, in seconds.
solution: Half the final energy means $I = I_f/\sqrt{2}$, since $U \propto I^2$. With $I = I_f(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ and $\tau = L/R = 0.050$ s, $e^{-t/\tau} = 1 - 1/\sqrt{2}$, so $t = \tau\ln[1/(1-1/\sqrt{2})] = 0.0614$ s.

name: Mutual inductance of two coaxial coils
statement: A large coil of $20$ turns and radius $0.20$ m has a small $100$-turn coil of radius $0.010$ m at its center, coaxial with it. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find the mutual inductance in henries.
solution: Run the current in the large coil: $B = \mu_0N_1I/(2R)$ is nearly uniform over the tiny coil, which links $N_2B\pi r^2$. So $M = \mu_0N_1N_2\pi r^2/(2R) = 1.9739e-06$ H. Mutual inductance is symmetric, so this works either direction.

name: Energy stored in a coaxial cable
statement: A coaxial cable has inner conductor radius $1.0$ mm and outer conductor radius $5.0$ mm, carrying $10$ A out along the inner conductor and back along the outer. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find the magnetic energy stored per meter of cable, in J/m.
solution: Between the conductors $B = \mu_0I/(2\pi r)$ and $u = B^2/(2\mu_0)$. Integrating over shells of volume $2\pi r\,dr$ per unit length gives $U/\ell = \frac{\mu_0I^2}{4\pi}\ln(b/a) = 1.6094e-05$ J/m.

name: Current when the charge is half its peak
statement: In an LC circuit with $L = 4.0$ mH and $C = 1.0\ \mu$F, the capacitor's maximum charge is $3.0\times10^{-6}$ C. Find the current at the instant the charge is half its maximum, in amperes.
solution: Energy conservation: $\frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$, so $I = \omega\sqrt{Q^2-q^2}$ with $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 15811$ rad/s. With $q = Q/2$, $I = \omega Q\sqrt{3}/2 = 0.0411$ A.

name: Voltage spike when the switch opens
statement: A $12$ V battery is in series with a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor; a $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor and an ideal inductor are connected in parallel with each other across the rest of the circuit. After a long time the switch is opened, cutting off the battery but leaving the inductor and the $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor in a closed loop. Find the magnitude of the voltage across the $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor immediately after the switch opens, in volts.
solution: At steady state the ideal inductor short-circuits the $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor, so the inductor carries $I = 12/4.0 = 3.0$ A. Inductor current cannot change instantly, so that same current is forced through the $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor: $V = IR = 18.0$ V.

name: Energy stored in a toroid
statement: A toroid with a rectangular cross-section has $1200$ turns, inner radius $0.060$ m, outer radius $0.090$ m, height $0.030$ m, and carries $2.0$ A. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A. Find the stored magnetic energy in joules.

name: Heat dissipated during one time constant
statement: A $10$ V battery, a $5.0\ \Omega$ resistor and a $0.50$ H inductor are connected in series at $t = 0$. Find the heat dissipated in the resistor between $t = 0$ and $t = \tau$, where $\tau = L/R$, in joules.
solution: With $I = I_0(1-e^{-t/\tau})$ and $I_0 = 2.0$ A, $Q = \int_0^\tau I^2R\,dt = I_0^2R\tau\left[\frac{3}{2} - 2e^{-1} + \frac{1}{2}e^{-2}\right]$. Numerically $I_0^2R\tau = 2.0$ J and the bracket is $0.83191$, giving $Q = 0.3362$ J.

name: Maximum current when two capacitors share charge
statement: A $4.0\ \mu$F capacitor charged to $20$ V is connected through a $2.0$ mH inductor to an identical uncharged $4.0\ \mu$F capacitor. Resistance is negligible. Find the maximum current that flows, in amperes.
solution: The current peaks when $dI/dt = 0$, i.e. when the inductor voltage is zero and the two capacitor voltages are equal, so each holds $Q_0/2 = 40.0\ \mu$C. Initial energy is $\frac{1}{2}C_1V_0^2 = 8.0e-04$ J and the capacitors then hold $4.0e-04$ J, so $\frac{1}{2}LI^2 = 4.0e-04$ J and $I = 0.632$ A.

name: Gas absorbs heat and expands
statement: A gas in a cylinder absorbs $Q = 850$ J of heat and does $W = 320$ J of work on its surroundings. Use $\Delta U = Q - W$. Find the change in internal energy in J.
solution: The first law is $\Delta U = Q - W$ with $W$ the work done BY the gas. So $\Delta U = 850 - 320 = 530$ J.

name: Work done on a compressed gas
statement: A gas is compressed, so the surroundings do 480 J of work on it. During the compression the gas releases 610 J of heat. Find $\Delta U$ for the gas in J.
solution: Work done BY the gas is $W = -480$ J and $Q = -610$ J. Then $\Delta U = Q - W = -610 + 480 = -130$ J, so the gas cools.

name: Isobaric expansion work
statement: A gas expands at a constant pressure of $2.00\times10^{5}$ Pa from $3.00\times10^{-3}$ m³ to $8.00\times10^{-3}$ m³. Find the work done by the gas in J.
solution: At constant pressure $W = P\,\Delta V$. So $W = (2.00\times10^{5})(5.00\times10^{-3}) = 1000$ J.

name: Isochoric heating
statement: A rigid sealed steel tank of gas is heated, absorbing 2400 J. Find the change in internal energy of the gas in J.
solution: A rigid container means $\Delta V = 0$, so $W = \int P\,dV = 0$. Then $\Delta U = Q = 2400$ J.

name: Isothermal ideal gas internal energy
statement: Two moles of an ideal monatomic gas expand isothermally at 300 K, absorbing 1500 J of heat. Find $\Delta U$ in J.
solution: For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$. The temperature is constant, so $\Delta U = 0$ (and all 1500 J goes into work).

name: Isothermal work of an ideal gas
statement: Three moles of an ideal gas at 350 K expand isothermally from 0.0200 m³ to 0.0600 m³. Use $R = 8.31$ J/mol·K. Find the work done by the gas in J.
solution: For an isothermal ideal gas, $W = \int P\,dV = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$. So $W = (3)(8.31)(350)\ln 3 \approx 9586$ J.

name: Heat in an isothermal expansion
statement: One mole of an ideal gas at 400 K expands isothermally until its volume doubles. Use $R = 8.31$ J/mol·K. Find the heat absorbed in J.
