statement: A siren radiates 0.80 W of sound uniformly in all directions over flat open ground, with no absorption. Using $I_0=1.0\times10^{-12}$ W/m$^2$, at what distance is the sound level 60 dB, in meters?
solution: A level of 60 dB means $I=I_0 10^{6}=1.0\times10^{-6}$ W/m$^2$. Setting $I=P/4\pi r^2$ gives $r=\sqrt{P/(4\pi I)}=\sqrt{0.80/(4\pi\times10^{-6})}=252$ m.

name: Energy in one wavelength
statement: A string with $\mu=0.020$ kg/m carries a sinusoidal wave of amplitude 0.010 m, angular frequency 100 rad/s, and wavelength 0.40 m. How much total (kinetic plus potential) wave energy is stored in one wavelength of the string, in joules?
solution: The energy per unit length averages $\tfrac12\mu\omega^2A^2$, so one wavelength holds $E=\tfrac12\mu\omega^2A^2\lambda$. That is $\tfrac12(0.020)(100)^2(0.010)^2(0.40)=4.0\times10^{-3}$ J.

name: Fundamental of a violin string
statement: A violin string of vibrating length 0.65 m carries transverse waves at 520 m/s. It is fixed at both ends. What is its fundamental frequency, in Hz?
solution: For a string fixed at both ends the fundamental fits half a wavelength, $\lambda_1=2L$, so $f_1=v/2L=520/1.30=400$ Hz.

name: Third harmonic
statement: A string fixed at both ends has a fundamental of 200 Hz. What is the frequency of its third harmonic, in Hz?
solution: A string fixed at both ends supports all integer multiples: $f_n=nf_1$. So $f_3=3(200)=600$ Hz.

name: Spacing of the nodes
statement: A standing wave on a string has wavelength 0.80 m. How far apart are adjacent nodes, in meters?
solution: Adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength: $\lambda/2=0.80/2=0.40$ m.

name: Open pipe fundamental
statement: An organ pipe 0.50 m long is open at both ends. Take the speed of sound to be 343 m/s and ignore the end correction. What is its fundamental frequency, in Hz?
solution: An open-open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so $\lambda_1=2L$ and $f_1=v/2L=343/1.00=343$ Hz.

name: Closed pipe fundamental
statement: A pipe 0.50 m long is open at one end and closed at the other. Sound travels at 343 m/s; ignore the end correction. What is its fundamental frequency, in Hz?
solution: A closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode, so the fundamental fits a quarter wavelength: $\lambda_1=4L$ and $f_1=v/4L=343/2.00=171.5$ Hz.

name: Next note a stopped pipe can sing
statement: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental of 100 Hz. What is the next-highest frequency at which it resonates, in Hz?
solution: A closed pipe only supports odd harmonics, $f_n=nf_1$ with $n=1,3,5,\dots$. The next one after 100 Hz is $3(100)=300$ Hz.

name: Counting nodes
statement: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its fourth harmonic. How many nodes does the standing wave have, counting the two fixed ends?
solution: The $n$th harmonic has $n$ antinodes and $n+1$ nodes including the ends. For $n=4$ that is 5 nodes.

name: Wavelength of a harmonic
statement: A string 1.2 m long is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its third harmonic. What is the wavelength of the standing wave, in meters?
solution: The $n$th harmonic fits $n$ half-wavelengths in $L$: $\lambda_n=2L/n=2(1.2)/3=0.80$ m.

name: Node to antinode
statement: A standing wave has wavelength 1.2 m. What is the distance from a node to the nearest antinode, in meters?
solution: Antinodes sit halfway between nodes, so the node-to-antinode distance is $\lambda/4=1.2/4=0.30$ m.

name: Sizing an open pipe
statement: How long must a pipe open at both ends be so that its fundamental is concert A, 440 Hz? Sound travels at 343 m/s; ignore the end correction. Give the length in meters.

name: Where to press for a fifth
statement: A guitar string has a vibrating length of 0.640 m from nut to bridge. A player presses it against a fret so the sounded pitch rises by a perfect fifth, a frequency ratio of 3:2. How far from the nut is that fret, in meters?
solution: Tension and $\mu$ are unchanged, so $v$ is fixed and $f_1=v/2L$ means $f\propto1/L$. Raising $f$ by 3/2 requires $L'=(2/3)(0.640)=0.4267$ m, so the fret sits $0.640-0.427=0.213$ m from the nut.

name: Tuning a string to A
statement: A string with linear density $1.20\times10^{-3}$ kg/m has a vibrating length of 0.640 m. What tension makes its fundamental 440 Hz, in newtons?

name: Two resonances in a tube
statement: A vertical tube stands in water and is driven by a 512 Hz fork at its open top. As the water level is lowered, resonances occur at a series of air-column lengths. Sound travels at 343 m/s. What is the distance between two successive resonance positions, in meters?
solution: Successive resonances of a closed tube differ by half a wavelength. With $\lambda=v/f=343/512=0.670$ m, the spacing is $\lambda/2=0.335$ m.

name: Frequency from the first resonance
statement: A resonance tube closed by water first resonates when the air column is 0.125 m long. Sound travels at 343 m/s and end corrections are ignored. What is the driving frequency, in Hz?
solution: The first resonance is the quarter-wave mode, $L=\lambda/4$, so $\lambda=0.500$ m and $f=v/\lambda=343/0.500=686$ Hz.

name: Harmonics below a cutoff
statement: A pipe open at both ends is 0.60 m long, with sound at 343 m/s. How many of its resonant frequencies lie below 1000 Hz?
solution: The open-open pipe has $f_1=v/2L=343/1.20=285.8$ Hz and all integer multiples: 285.8, 571.7, 857.5, 1143 Hz. Three of them fall below 1000 Hz.

name: Fifth harmonic of a stopped pipe
statement: A pipe of length 0.85 m is closed at one end. Sound travels at 343 m/s. What is the frequency of its $n=5$ mode, in Hz?
solution: For a closed pipe $f_n=nv/4L$ with odd $n$. So $f_5=5(343)/(4\times0.85)=5(100.9)=504$ Hz.

name: An organ pipe in a warm church
statement: An organ pipe sounds 350 Hz at $20^\circ$C. The speed of sound scales as $\sqrt{T}$ with $T$ in kelvin. What does the pipe sound at $35^\circ$C, in Hz?
solution: The pipe length sets $\lambda$, so $f\propto v\propto\sqrt{T}$. Then $f=350\sqrt{308.15/293.15}=350(1.0252)=358.8$ Hz. The pipe goes sharp as the room warms.

name: String with one free end
statement: A 1.50 m string is clamped at one end; the other end is attached to a light ring that slides freely on a frictionless rod, so it is a displacement antinode. Waves travel at 60 m/s. What is the fundamental frequency, in Hz?
solution: A fixed-free string fits a quarter wavelength in its fundamental: $\lambda_1=4L=6.0$ m, so $f_1=v/\lambda_1=60/6.0=10$ Hz.

name: Next mode of the fixed-free string
statement: A 1.50 m string is clamped at one end, with the other end free to slide on a frictionless rod (a displacement antinode there). Its fundamental frequency is 10.0 Hz. What is its next resonant frequency, in Hz?
solution: A fixed-free boundary pair, like a stopped pipe, allows only odd multiples: $f_n=nf_1$ with $n=1,3,5,\dots$. The next is $3(10.0)=30.0$ Hz.

name: Fundamental from two neighbours
statement: A string fixed at both ends resonates at 420 Hz and again at 490 Hz, with no resonance in between. What is its fundamental frequency, in Hz?
solution: For a string all harmonics are present, so consecutive resonances differ by exactly $f_1$. Thus $f_1=490-420=70$ Hz.

name: Fundamental of a stopped pipe
statement: A pipe closed at one end resonates at 750 Hz and at 1050 Hz, with nothing in between. What is its fundamental frequency, in Hz?
solution: Only odd harmonics exist, so consecutive resonances differ by $2f_1$. Then $2f_1=1050-750=300$ Hz, giving $f_1=150$ Hz. Check: 750 and 1050 are the 5th and 7th harmonics.

name: A wire on a sonometer
statement: A wire 0.80 m long between two bridges has a mass of 3.2 g and is stretched to 200 N. What is its fundamental frequency, in Hz?

name: Matching a pipe to a string
statement: A string fixed at both ends sounds a fundamental of 256 Hz. How long must a pipe open at both ends be to sound the same fundamental? Sound in air travels at 343 m/s; ignore end corrections. Give the length in meters.
solution: The string's own length and wave speed do not matter, only the frequency it produces. For the air column, $f_1=v_{air}/2L$, so $L=343/(2\times256)=0.670$ m. The wave speed in air, not in the string, sets the pipe length.

name: Counting resonances as the water drops
statement: A tube 1.00 m long stands vertically and is initially full of water. A 440 Hz fork is held over the open top while the water is slowly drained all the way out. Sound travels at 343 m/s and end corrections are ignored. How many resonances are heard?
solution: The air column above the water acts as a closed pipe, resonating when $L=(2n-1)\lambda/4$. With $\lambda=343/440=0.780$ m the quarter wavelength is 0.195 m, so resonances occur at 0.195 m, 0.585 m, and 0.974 m. The next would need 1.364 m, longer than the tube, so 3 resonances are heard.

name: Length from a harmonic
statement: A string fixed at both ends carries waves at 440 m/s and its third harmonic is 660 Hz. How long is the string, in meters?
solution: For the $n$th harmonic $f_n=nv/2L$, so $L=nv/2f_n=3(440)/(2\times660)=1.00$ m.

name: A pipe driving a string
statement: A pipe 0.32 m long, closed at one end, is sounded at its fundamental with sound at 343 m/s. A string 0.40 m long with $\mu=2.5\times10^{-3}$ kg/m, fixed at both ends, resonates in its fundamental with that tone. What is the string's tension, in newtons?
solution: The pipe gives $f=v/4L_p=343/1.28=268.0$ Hz. The string must have the same fundamental, so $T=\mu(2L_sf)^2=(2.5\times10^{-3})(0.80\times268.0)^2=115$ N.

name: Identifying the mode
statement: A string 1.2 m long, fixed at both ends, is driven so that its nodes are 0.20 m apart. Its fundamental is 55 Hz. What is the driving frequency, in Hz?
solution: Node spacing is $\lambda/2$, so $\lambda=0.40$ m and the number of half-wavelengths is $n=2L/\lambda=2(1.2)/0.40=6$. The string is in its 6th harmonic, $f=6(55)=330$ Hz.

name: Warming a pipe into tune
statement: A pipe 0.25 m long and closed at one end must sound exactly 350 Hz. The speed of sound in air is $v=331\sqrt{T/273.15}$ m/s with $T$ in kelvin. At what air temperature does the pipe hit that frequency, in $^\circ$C?

name: Plugging one end
statement: A pipe open at both ends has a fundamental of 300 Hz. One end is then sealed, leaving the length unchanged. What is the highest resonant frequency of the sealed pipe that lies below 1200 Hz, in Hz?
solution: Sealing one end changes $\lambda_1$ from $2L$ to $4L$, so the fundamental halves to 150 Hz, and only odd harmonics survive: 150, 450, 750, 1050, 1350 Hz. The largest below 1200 Hz is 1050 Hz.

name: Mass that tunes the wire
statement: A wire of linear density $1.8\times10^{-3}$ kg/m runs 0.60 m between two bridges and passes over a pulley to a hanging mass. It resonates in its second harmonic when driven by a 400 Hz fork. Take $g=9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the hanging mass, in kilograms?
solution: The second harmonic is $f_2=(2/2L)\sqrt{T/\mu}=(1/L)\sqrt{T/\mu}$, so $\sqrt{T/\mu}=f_2L=240$ m/s and $T=\mu(240)^2=103.7$ N. The hanging weight supplies that tension, so $m=T/g=103.7/9.8=10.6$ kg.

name: Two forks side by side
statement: A 440 Hz tuning fork and a 443 Hz tuning fork are struck at the same time. What beat frequency does a listener hear, in Hz?
solution: Beats occur at $f_\text{beat}=|f_1-f_2|$. Here $|443-440|=3$ Hz, so the loudness rises and falls 3 times each second.

name: Time between loud moments
statement: Tuning forks of 512 Hz and 508 Hz sound together. How much time passes between one loud moment and the next, in s?
solution: The beat frequency is $|512-508|=4$ Hz, and the time between loudness maxima is the beat period $T=1/f_\text{beat}=1/4=0.25$ s.

name: A flat piano string
statement: A piano string sounded with a 440 Hz tuning fork produces 3 beats per second. The string is known to be flat (lower in frequency than the fork). What is the string's frequency, in Hz?
solution: Beats give $|f_\text{string}-440|=3$, so the string is at 437 Hz or 443 Hz. Because it is flat, $f_\text{string}=437$ Hz.

name: Counting beats over ten seconds
statement: Two tuning forks sounded together produce 20 beats in 10.0 s. One fork is 256 Hz and the other has the higher frequency. What is the frequency of the second fork, in Hz?
solution: The beat frequency is $20/10.0=2.0$ Hz, so $|f_2-256|=2.0$ Hz. Since $f_2$ is the higher one, $f_2=258$ Hz.

name: Phase from a path difference
statement: Two speakers driven in phase emit 343 Hz sound. Take the speed of sound to be 343 m/s. At one point the two paths differ in length by 2.50 m. What is the phase difference between the two waves at that point, in rad?
solution: The wavelength is $\lambda=v/f=343/343=1.00$ m. Phase difference follows $\Delta\phi=2\pi\,\Delta r/\lambda=2\pi(2.50/1.00)=5\pi\approx15.71$ rad.

name: Smallest constructive path difference
statement: Two speakers driven in phase emit 686 Hz sound; the speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the smallest nonzero path difference that gives constructive interference, in m?
solution: Constructive interference for in-phase sources needs $\Delta r=m\lambda$. With $\lambda=343/686=0.500$ m, the smallest nonzero case is $m=1$, so $\Delta r=0.500$ m.

name: First quiet spot
statement: Two speakers driven in phase emit 1715 Hz sound; the speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the smallest path difference that produces destructive interference, in m?
solution: Destructive interference for in-phase sources needs $\Delta r=(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$. With $\lambda=343/1715=0.200$ m the smallest value is $\lambda/2=0.100$ m.

name: Adding two waves out of step
statement: Two sound waves of the same frequency each have displacement amplitude 3.0 mm and arrive at a point with a phase difference of $60^\circ$. The resultant amplitude is $2A\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$. What is the resultant amplitude, in mm?
solution: Using $2A\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$ with $A=3.0$ mm and $\Delta\phi=60^\circ$: $2(3.0)\cos 30^\circ=6.0(0.866)=5.20$ mm.

name: Phase lag over 30 centimeters
statement: A 500 Hz sound travels at 343 m/s. Two paths from a pair of in-phase speakers to a microphone differ by 0.30 m. What is the phase difference of the two arriving waves, in rad?
solution: $\lambda=343/500=0.686$ m, and $\Delta\phi=2\pi\,\Delta r/\lambda=2\pi(0.30/0.686)=2.75$ rad.

name: Speakers wired backwards
statement: Two speakers emit 343 Hz sound but are wired so that they are exactly out of phase ($\pi$ rad apart). The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the smallest path difference that gives constructive interference, in m?
solution: The built-in $\pi$ phase flip means the roles of maxima and minima swap: constructive interference requires $\Delta r=(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$. With $\lambda=1.00$ m, the smallest value is 0.500 m.

name: Which way did the tuner turn?
statement: A tuner sounds a piano string with a 440 Hz fork and hears 4 beats per second. After tightening the string slightly, the beat rate rises to 6 per second. Tightening a string raises its frequency. What was the string's original frequency, in Hz?
solution: Originally $f=436$ Hz or $444$ Hz. Tightening raises $f$; from 444 Hz the beat rate would fall, from 436 Hz it would rise. The rate rose, so the string started at 436 Hz.

name: Two guitar strings
statement: Two guitar strings played together give 5 beats in 2.0 s. One string is tuned to 196.0 Hz and the other is slightly flat. What is the frequency of the flat string, in Hz?
solution: The beat frequency is $5/2.0=2.5$ Hz, so the strings differ by 2.5 Hz. The flat string is lower: $196.0-2.5=193.5$ Hz.

name: Lowest frequency for silence
statement: Two speakers on a wall are 2.0 m apart and driven in phase by the same amplifier. A listener stands 4.0 m straight out from the lower speaker, so the perpendicular from that speaker passes through her ear. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the lowest frequency for which she hears destructive interference, in Hz?
solution: The path difference is $\Delta r=\sqrt{4.0^2+2.0^2}-4.0=4.472-4.000=0.472$ m. Destructive interference needs $\Delta r=\lambda/2$ at lowest order, so $\lambda=0.944$ m and $f=343/0.944=363$ Hz.

name: Lowest frequency for a maximum
statement: Two in-phase speakers are 2.0 m apart; a listener stands 4.0 m along the perpendicular from one of them. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the lowest nonzero frequency at which she hears constructive interference, in Hz?
solution: The path difference is $\Delta r=\sqrt{4.0^2+2.0^2}-4.0=0.472$ m. Constructive interference needs $\Delta r=\lambda$ at lowest nonzero order, so $f=v/\Delta r=343/0.472=727$ Hz.

name: A drifting speaker
statement: Two identical speakers each emit 500 Hz. One sits on a table; the other is carried directly away from a listener at 2.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What beat frequency does the listener hear, in Hz?
solution: The receding speaker is heard at $f'=f\,v/(v+v_s)=500(343)/345=497.10$ Hz. The beat frequency is $|500-497.10|=2.90$ Hz.

name: Spacing of quiet points
statement: Two speakers face each other across a room and emit 686 Hz sound in phase; the speed of sound is 343 m/s. Walking along the line between them, a listener passes through alternating loud and quiet points. What is the distance between adjacent quiet points, in m?
solution: Along the line the two waves form a standing-wave pattern. Nodes are spaced by $\lambda/2$, and $\lambda=343/686=0.500$ m, so adjacent quiet points are 0.250 m apart.

name: Working backwards to the phase
statement: Two waves of equal amplitude 4.0 mm combine to give a resultant of amplitude 4.0 mm, using $2A\cos(\Delta\phi/2)$. What is the phase difference between them, in rad? (Give the smallest positive value.)
solution: Set $2(4.0)\cos(\Delta\phi/2)=4.0$, so $\cos(\Delta\phi/2)=0.500$ and $\Delta\phi/2=\pi/3$. Hence $\Delta\phi=2\pi/3=2.09$ rad.

name: Sliding tube interferometer
statement: In a Quincke tube, sound splits into two paths and recombines. Pulling the sliding U-section out by 0.15 m lengthens one path by 0.30 m (the extra length is traversed twice). Starting from equal paths, this produces the first minimum at the detector. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the frequency of the sound, in Hz?
solution: The first minimum occurs when the extra path equals $\lambda/2$, so $\lambda=2(0.30)=0.60$ m. Then $f=v/\lambda=343/0.60=572$ Hz.

name: Successive minima in the tube
statement: In a Quincke tube the slider is moved steadily and successive minima are found 0.25 m apart in slider position, which corresponds to 0.50 m of extra path each time. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the frequency, in Hz?
solution: Successive minima are separated by one full wavelength of extra path, so $\lambda=0.50$ m and $f=343/0.50=686$ Hz.

name: Two organ pipes
statement: Two open organ pipes have lengths 0.500 m and 0.510 m. Each sounds its fundamental, $f=v/2L$, with $v=343$ m/s. What beat frequency is heard, in Hz?
solution: The fundamentals are $343/(2\cdot0.500)=343.0$ Hz and $343/(2\cdot0.510)=336.27$ Hz. The beat frequency is the difference, $6.73$ Hz.

name: One pipe in a warm room
statement: Two identical open pipes are 0.600 m long, with fundamental $f=v/2L$. One sits in air where sound travels at 343 m/s; the other is in a warmer alcove where sound travels at 349 m/s. What beat frequency results, in Hz?
solution: The fundamentals are $343/1.20=285.8$ Hz and $349/1.20=290.8$ Hz. The beat frequency is $\Delta f=\Delta v/2L=6.0/1.20=5.00$ Hz.

name: String against a fork
statement: A string 0.650 m long is fixed at both ends and carries waves at 260 m/s, so its fundamental is $f=v/2L$. It is sounded with a 203 Hz tuning fork. What beat frequency is heard, in Hz?
solution: The string's fundamental is $260/(2\cdot0.650)=200$ Hz. Beating with the 203 Hz fork gives $|203-200|=3.00$ Hz.

name: Two percent more tension
statement: A string tuned to exactly 440 Hz has its tension increased by 2.00%. The frequency of a string scales as $f\propto\sqrt{T}$. It is then sounded with a 440 Hz fork. What beat frequency is heard, in Hz?
solution: Since $f\propto\sqrt{T}$, the new frequency is $440\sqrt{1.0200}=444.38$ Hz. The beat frequency is $444.38-440=4.38$ Hz.

name: How many silent tones
statement: Two speakers on a wall are 4.00 m apart and driven in phase. A listener stands 3.00 m straight out from one speaker, so the paths are 3.00 m and 5.00 m. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. How many frequencies below 1000 Hz give destructive interference at her ear?
solution: The path difference is fixed at $\Delta r=5.00-3.00=2.00$ m. Destructive interference needs $\Delta r=(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$, i.e. $f=(n+\tfrac12)v/\Delta r=(n+\tfrac12)(171.5)$ Hz. Values 85.8, 257, 429, 600, 772, 943 Hz lie below 1000 Hz, so there are 6.

name: Counting quiet directions
statement: Two speakers 2.00 m apart are driven in phase at 1029 Hz ($v=343$ m/s). A listener walks once around them on a large circle far away. The path difference varies continuously from $-2.00$ m to $+2.00$ m and back. How many quiet directions does she pass through in one full loop?
solution: Here $\lambda=343/1029=0.3333$ m, so $d/\lambda=6.00$. Minima need $\Delta r=(m+\tfrac12)\lambda$ with $|\Delta r|<2.00$ m, i.e. $m+\tfrac12=0.5,1.5,\dots,5.5$: six values on each side of the axis, 12 in all.

name: Siren on an approaching car
statement: Two identical sirens each emit 400 Hz. One is fixed beside the road; the other is on a car approaching a stationary listener at 15.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What beat frequency does the listener hear, in Hz?
solution: The approaching siren is heard at $f'=f\,v/(v-v_s)=400(343)/328=418.29$ Hz. Beating against the fixed 400 Hz siren gives $18.3$ Hz.

name: How much to tighten
statement: A violin string sounds 3.0 beats per second against a 440 Hz fork and is flat. Since $f\propto\sqrt{T}$, by what percentage must the tension be increased to bring it into tune? Give the answer in percent.
solution: Flat by 3.0 Hz means $f=437$ Hz. Tension scales as $T\propto f^2$, so $T_\text{new}/T=(440/437)^2=1.0138$, an increase of 1.38%.

name: Out-of-phase speakers at an odd point
statement: Two speakers emit 343 Hz sound ($v=343$ m/s) but are driven exactly out of phase. Each alone would produce displacement amplitude 1.00 mm at a listener whose two path lengths differ by 0.750 m. Using $2A|\cos(\Delta\phi/2)|$, what is the resultant amplitude, in mm?
solution: With $\lambda=1.00$ m, the path difference contributes $2\pi(0.750)=1.5\pi$ and the wiring adds $\pi$, so $\Delta\phi=2.5\pi$. Then $2(1.00)|\cos(1.25\pi)|=2(0.7071)=1.41$ mm.

name: Beats against a wall
statement: A 500 Hz buzzer moves toward a flat wall at 3.00 m/s. A listener stands well behind the buzzer, in line with its motion, and hears both the direct sound and the sound reflected from the wall. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What beat frequency does she hear, in Hz?
solution: The direct sound comes from a source receding from her: $500(343)/346=495.66$ Hz. The reflection acts like an image source approaching her at 3.00 m/s: $500(343)/340=504.41$ Hz. The beat frequency is the difference, $8.75$ Hz.

name: Walking to the first quiet spot
statement: Two speakers 3.00 m apart on a wall are driven in phase at 500 Hz ($v=343$ m/s). A listener walks along a straight line 4.00 m from the wall and parallel to it, starting on the perpendicular bisector. How far must she walk to reach the first point of destructive interference, in m?
solution: With $\lambda=343/500=0.686$ m, the first minimum needs $\sqrt{(x+1.5)^2+4^2}-\sqrt{(x-1.5)^2+4^2}=\lambda/2=0.343$ m. Solving numerically gives $x=0.491$ m. The far-field estimate $x\approx\lambda L/2d=0.457$ m is close but not exact, since 4.00 m is not large compared with the 3.00 m separation.

name: Ambulance approaching
statement: An ambulance siren emits 800 Hz and the ambulance drives toward a stationary listener at 25.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear, in Hz?

name: Ambulance receding
statement: The same ambulance, siren at 800 Hz, has passed and now recedes at 25.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear, in Hz?
solution: For a receding source, $f'=f\,v/(v+v_s)=800(343)/368=746$ Hz. The pitch drops below 800 Hz once the ambulance passes.

name: Running toward a speaker
statement: A speaker at rest emits 500 Hz. A cyclist rides straight toward it at 20.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the cyclist hear, in Hz?
solution: For a moving observer and stationary source, $f'=f(v+v_o)/v=500(363)/343=529$ Hz.

name: Riding away from a speaker
statement: A stationary speaker emits 500 Hz. A car drives directly away from it at 30.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency do the occupants hear, in Hz?
solution: For an observer moving away, $f'=f(v-v_o)/v=500(313)/343=456$ Hz.

name: Train horn
statement: A train horn sounds at 300 Hz while the train approaches a crossing at 40.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does someone waiting at the crossing hear, in Hz?

name: Car horn fading
statement: A car sounding a 440 Hz horn drives away from a pedestrian at 15.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the pedestrian hear, in Hz?

name: How big is the shift
statement: A police siren emits 1200 Hz from a car approaching at 30.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. By how much is the heard frequency raised above 1200 Hz, in Hz?
solution: The heard frequency is $1200(343)/313=1315.0$ Hz, so the shift is $1315.0-1200=115$ Hz.

name: Jogger and a loudspeaker
statement: A loudspeaker at rest plays a steady 600 Hz tone. A jogger runs straight at it at 8.00 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the jogger hear, in Hz?

name: One-tenth the speed of sound
statement: A source emitting 1000 Hz moves toward a stationary observer at 34.3 m/s, one-tenth the 343 m/s speed of sound. What frequency is heard, in Hz?
solution: $f'=f\,v/(v-v_s)=1000(343)/308.7=1111$ Hz. Note the shift is about 11%, not 10%, because the factor is $1/(1-0.1)$.

name: Whistle on a departing train
statement: A 2000 Hz whistle sits on a train pulling away from the platform at 20.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does a person on the platform hear, in Hz?

name: Both in motion, closing
statement: A 500 Hz siren on a truck moves at 25.0 m/s toward a motorcyclist who rides at 10.0 m/s toward the truck. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the motorcyclist hear, in Hz?
solution: Use $f'=f(v+v_o)/(v-v_s)$ with both motions closing the gap: $500(343+10)/(343-25)=500(353)/318=555$ Hz.

name: Chasing a source
statement: A 400 Hz horn is on a van moving away from a car at 20.0 m/s, while the car chases it at 15.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency do the people in the car hear, in Hz?
solution: Take the direction from source to observer as reference: the source recedes and the observer pursues, so $f'=f(v+v_o)/(v+v_s)=400(358)/363=394$ Hz. The pitch is still slightly low because the gap is widening.

name: A tailwind from source to listener
statement: A 500 Hz source approaches a stationary listener at 25.0 m/s. A steady 10.0 m/s wind blows from the source toward the listener. In still air sound travels at 343 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear, in Hz?
solution: Wind shifts the sound speed in the ground frame to $v+w=353$ m/s for both source and listener: $f'=f(v+w)/(v+w-v_s)=500(353)/328=538$ Hz.

name: The same source into a headwind
statement: The same 500 Hz source approaches the same stationary listener at 25.0 m/s, but now a 10.0 m/s wind blows from the listener toward the source. Still-air sound speed is 343 m/s. What frequency is heard, in Hz?
solution: Now the effective sound speed toward the listener is $v-w=333$ m/s: $f'=500(333)/(333-25)=500(333)/308=541$ Hz. Wind changes the answer because it changes $v$ in both numerator and denominator unequally.

name: Speed from the pitch drop
statement: As an ambulance passes, a bystander hears the siren drop from 870 Hz to 800 Hz. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. How fast is the ambulance moving, in m/s?
solution: Approaching gives $f_1=fv/(v-u)$ and receding $f_2=fv/(v+u)$, so $f_1/f_2=(v+u)/(v-u)$. With the ratio $870/800=1.0875$, $u=v(R-1)/(R+1)=343(0.0875)/(2.0875)=14.4$ m/s.

name: The siren's true pitch
statement: The same ambulance siren is heard at 870 Hz approaching and 800 Hz receding. What is the siren's actual emitted frequency, in Hz?
solution: From $f_1=fv/(v-u)$ and $f_2=fv/(v+u)$, adding the reciprocals gives $1/f_1+1/f_2=2/f$, so $f$ is the harmonic mean: $f=2f_1f_2/(f_1+f_2)=2(870)(800)/1670=834$ Hz.

name: Bat closing on a moth
statement: A bat at rest emits a 40.0 kHz call. A moth flies straight toward the bat at 6.00 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the moth receive, in Hz?
solution: The moth is a moving observer, source at rest: $f'=f(v+v_o)/v=40000(349)/343=40700$ Hz.

name: Echo from a wall
statement: A 500 Hz horn on a cart moves toward a flat wall at 10.0 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency of the reflected sound does a microphone riding on the cart detect, in Hz?
solution: The wall receives $f_1=fv/(v-u)$ as a moving-source shift, then re-emits it at rest; the cart is an observer moving toward it, adding a second factor. The result is $f''=f(v+u)/(v-u)=500(353)/333=530$ Hz.

name: Sound radar on a car
statement: A stationary transmitter emits 1000 Hz toward a car approaching it at 20.0 m/s; the sound reflects off the car and returns. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency comes back to the transmitter, in Hz?
solution: The car first acts as a moving observer, $f_1=f(v+u)/v$, then as a moving source of $f_1$, giving $f_2=f_1 v/(v-u)$. Combined, $f_2=f(v+u)/(v-u)=1000(363)/323=1124$ Hz.

name: Two trains meeting
statement: Train A sounds a 350 Hz horn and travels at 25.0 m/s toward train B, which travels at 15.0 m/s toward A on a parallel track. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does a passenger on B hear, in Hz?
solution: Both motions close the gap: $f'=f(v+v_o)/(v-v_s)=350(358)/318=394$ Hz.

name: Whirling siren, highest pitch
statement: A 500 Hz buzzer is whirled on a 1.00 m string at 2.00 revolutions per second. A listener stands far away in the plane of the circle. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What is the highest frequency heard, in Hz?
solution: The buzzer's speed is $v_s=2\pi r f_\text{rot}=2\pi(1.00)(2.00)=12.57$ m/s. The maximum occurs when it moves straight at the listener: $f'=500(343)/(343-12.57)=519$ Hz.

name: Whirling siren, lowest pitch
statement: The same 500 Hz buzzer whirls on a 1.00 m string at 2.00 rev/s, heard from far away in the plane of the circle ($v=343$ m/s). What is the lowest frequency heard, in Hz?
solution: The minimum occurs when the buzzer moves directly away: $f'=fv/(v+v_s)=500(343)/(343+12.57)=482$ Hz. Note the maximum and minimum are not symmetric about 500 Hz.

name: Mach cone angle
statement: A jet flies at Mach 2.00. The shock cone half-angle satisfies $\sin\theta=1/M$. What is the half-angle of the cone, in degrees?
solution: $\sin\theta=1/M=0.500$, so $\theta=30.0^\circ$. Faster aircraft make narrower cones.

name: Speed from the cone
statement: The shock cone from an aircraft has half-angle $25.0^\circ$, with $\sin\theta=1/M$. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. How fast is the aircraft flying, in m/s?

name: Waiting for the boom
statement: A plane flies level at 8000 m altitude at Mach 1.50 ($v=343$ m/s), passing directly overhead. The shock cone half-angle obeys $\sin\theta=1/M$. How long after the plane passes overhead does the observer hear the sonic boom, in s?
solution: The cone half-angle is $\theta=\arcsin(1/1.50)=41.8^\circ$, so the cone reaches the ground once the plane is a horizontal distance $h/\tan\theta=8000/0.894=8944$ m past the observer. At $1.50(343)=514.5$ m/s that takes $17.4$ s.

name: Bat closing on a wall
statement: A bat flies toward a cave wall at 5.00 m/s while emitting a steady 50.0 kHz call. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What beat frequency does the bat detect between its own call and the returning echo, in Hz?
solution: The echo comes back double-shifted: $f''=f(v+u)/(v-u)=50000(348)/338=51479$ Hz. Beating against the emitted 50000 Hz gives $1.48\times10^3$ Hz — bats use exactly this to judge closing speed.

name: Reflecting off a moving panel
statement: A stationary speaker emits 2000 Hz at a large flat panel that moves toward the speaker at 5.00 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does a microphone at the speaker detect in the reflected sound, in Hz?
solution: The panel receives $f(v+u)/v$ as a moving observer and re-radiates it as a moving source, giving $f''=f(v+u)/(v-u)=2000(348)/338=2059$ Hz.

name: The moment of closest approach
statement: An ambulance with a 700 Hz siren drives at 30.0 m/s along a straight road. A pedestrian stands 20.0 m from the road. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does she hear from the sound emitted at the instant the ambulance is closest to her, in Hz?
solution: Only the component of source velocity along the line to the listener matters. At closest approach the velocity is perpendicular to that line, so the radial component is zero and there is no shift: she hears 700 Hz. (She hears it a moment later, after the pitch has already begun dropping in other sound.)

name: Redshift of a star
statement: A hydrogen line emitted at 656.3 nm is observed at 658.0 nm in the spectrum of a distant star. For speeds far below $c=3.00\times10^8$ m/s, $\Delta\lambda/\lambda\approx v/c$. How fast is the star receding, in km/s?
solution: $\Delta\lambda/\lambda=1.7/656.3=2.590\times10^{-3}$, so $v=(2.590\times10^{-3})(3.00\times10^8)=7.77\times10^5$ m/s, or 777 km/s. The line moves to longer wavelength, so the star is moving away.

name: Two trains and a wind
statement: Train A moves east at 30.0 m/s sounding a 400 Hz horn. Train B is east of A and moves west at 20.0 m/s, so they approach. A steady 10.0 m/s wind blows east. Still-air sound speed is 343 m/s. What frequency does a passenger on B hear, in Hz?
solution: Work in the air's frame, where the Doppler formula holds with $v=343$ m/s. Relative to the air the source moves east at $30-10=20$ m/s and the observer moves west at $20+10=30$ m/s. Sound travels eastward, so $f'=f(v+30)/(v-20)=400(373)/323=462$ Hz.
